method: Each walkthrough comes from questioning the use case's NotebookLM notebook. The notebook's sources are the Seeq use case page, related Seeq pages, and the Seeq Knowledge Base page for every tool used. Formula examples were then checked against the Knowledge Base.

cases.title: Pump health monitoring
problem: A large US oil and gas operator runs hundreds of centrifugal pumps. Pumps were either run until they broke, costing about 10 hours of unplanned downtime per failure plus rush repairs and lost production, or serviced on a fixed calendar, which wasted work on healthy pumps.
Nobody could see the health of the whole fleet, because hundreds of multi-tag time series are too much for spreadsheets.
Data available: process signals such as flow, motor power, pressures and vibration in the OSIsoft PI historian; work orders and asset records in Maximo; lab results in the LIMS.
cases.solution: Condition-based monitoring. Clean each pump's signals, keep only the time it is actually running, and measure two things every day: the percentage of running time spent in a poor operating mode, and how far the pump went past its limits. Combine the two into a daily health score for every pump, rank the fleet on a scorecard, and plan maintenance for the pumps that are sliding.

steps.inputs: Raw flow, vibration or pressure signal from PI
steps.settings: Filter type: Seeq Agile Filter. Keep the default window (33 × sample period) to start.
steps.why: Noise and dropouts would otherwise trigger false poor-mode alerts later.

steps.inputs: Smoothed flow signal
steps.settings: Replace negative flow readings with zero.
steps.why: Flow meters read slightly negative when a pump stops; negative flow breaks later maths.

steps.n: Find when the pump is running
steps.inputs: Corrected flow (or motor power)
steps.settings: is greater than 0.5 m³/h; set a short-gap filter so brief blips don't split capsules.
steps.why: Idle time must be excluded, or a stopped pump looks healthy.

steps.inputs: Vibration, pressure difference, flow; Pump Running
steps.settings: One Value Search per limit (e.g. vibration above its alarm level, flow below minimum flow). Combine with Pump Running using intersection (AND).
steps.why: Marks exactly when the pump runs outside its design envelope.

steps.inputs: Poor Operating Mode; violation signal; daily capsules
steps.settings: Periodic Condition: Daily, in the site time zone. Signal from Condition statistics: Percent Duration (time in poor mode) and Average or Totalized (size of the violation). Timestamp at capsule start, step interpolation.
steps.output: Two daily signals: % time in poor mode, violation magnitude
steps.why: A score needs numbers per day, not a scatter of events.

steps.inputs: Process signal and the operating-mode conditions
steps.settings: Aggregate by condition; statistic Percent or Total Duration.
steps.output: Chart of time in stopped, good and poor modes
steps.why: Shows engineers where each pump spends its life.

steps.inputs: The two daily signals from step 5
steps.settings: Combine into one score on a 0–100 scale. Seeq does not publish the weights; tune them to your failure history.
steps.output: Daily Pump Health Score for each pump
steps.why: One comparable number lets you rank hundreds of pumps.

steps.inputs: Health Score, daily capsules
steps.settings: Value at end of day; colour thresholds, e.g. green ≥ 80, yellow 60–80, red < 60.
steps.why: Bad actors stand out at a glance.

steps.inputs: Worksheets, scorecard, histograms
steps.settings: Daily auto-refresh; record each analysis step in the Journal.
steps.why: Operations, reliability and IT all work from the same trusted numbers.

example.caption: Pump P-101, one day
rows: Time in poor mode (step 4: running AND vibration above 4.5 mm/s)
% of running time in poor mode (step 5)

mistakes: Working out percentages over the whole day instead of running time
If the pump was off for 12 hours, its poor-mode share halves and hides the problem. Always bound the calculations by Pump Running.
Smoothing too hard
A wide filter flattens the short vibration spikes you are looking for. Start from the default window and overlay raw and smoothed signals before you trust them.
Adding signals with different units
Formula refuses to add mm/s to °C, and even if it didn't, the result would mean nothing. Convert each indicator to a percentage first, then combine.
cases.reported: Lower chance of pump failure and of the associated production loss; maintenance done only when needed; operations and IT aligned on one data set; plans to extend to other critical assets. The page quantifies only the baseline of about 10 hours of downtime per failure.
cases.assumptions: Tag names, the 0.5 m³/h running limit, the vibration limit, the score weights and the colour thresholds are not stated by Seeq. They are placeholders to be set per site.

cases.title: Golden batch monitoring for OEE improvement
problem: Cabot's inkjet dispersion plant runs several batch lines, each with 4 to 6 unit operations in sequence. One operator watches several units while answering control-system prompts and doing field tasks.

Small waits add up: answering a prompt late, waiting for a downstream vessel, picking which unit to serve next. Together they cost 5% or more of overall equipment effectiveness (OEE). Standard OEE records only batch start and end, so none of this shows.
Data available: process signals and batch context (grade, batch number, phase times) from the DCS historian; lab results from LIMS or SQL.
cases.solution: Build a golden batch: a typical profile with tolerance bands, taken from known good batches. Compare every live batch against it in real time, and flag two kinds of lost time: excursions outside the bands inside a batch, and unexplained gaps between batches. Show operators what each unit will need next, so OEE becomes a live steering tool instead of a monthly report.

steps.inputs: Unit state tag, motor power or valve position
steps.settings: Entry rule such as state equals 'Production'; a maximum capsule length; short-gap filter.
steps.output: Condition: one capsule per unit operation
steps.why: Separates processing time from idle time.

steps.inputs: Batch condition and lab quality results
steps.settings: Pick about five batches with good quality and no equipment faults. Trim them to the same length (for example the first 12 hours) so they line up.
steps.why: The reference is only as good as the batches it learns from.

steps.n: Build the golden profile and bands
steps.inputs: Key signal (e.g. reactor temperature), Best Production Runs, training window, gridding period (e.g. 5 min)
steps.settings: Centre line: Average. Bands: ±3 standard deviations or ±2 average deviations. Apply to future batches.
steps.output: Three signals: golden profile, upper limit, lower limit
steps.why: Gives limits that follow the shape of the batch rather than one flat alarm line.

steps.inputs: Live signal, the two limits, active batch condition
steps.settings: Flag when the live signal is above the upper or below the lower limit during a batch. Separately, flag the time between one batch ending and the next starting.
steps.why: Splits lost time into process instability and idle equipment.

steps.inputs: Excursion and delay conditions; shift or daily capsules
steps.settings: Total Duration (minutes lost) and Count (number of events); colour thresholds.
steps.output: Lost-time KPIs and a colour table
steps.why: Turns what you can see on a trend into numbers for OEE accounting.

steps.n: Copy to every line and grade
steps.inputs: Finished worksheet; tags mapped as Line → Unit → Signal
steps.settings: Build once on one unit, then swap assets.
steps.output: The same analysis on all lines
steps.why: About one month to build the first, then quick to extend.

steps.n: Put it in front of operators
steps.inputs: Worksheets and scorecards
steps.settings: Auto-refresh; a 12-hour view for the shift and a 48-hour view for the daily review.
steps.why: Operators see what each unit needs 5 to 30 minutes ahead.

example.caption: Reactor 101, one 12-hour shift (720 min)
example.note: Counting excursion minutes as lost time is a simplification for teaching. The batch keeps running during an excursion, but it is running off-profile.

mistakes: Training on batches of different lengths
The bands smear because phases don't line up. Trim the training batches to a common length first.
No short-gap filter on the step search
Brief signal dips split one batch into dozens of capsules and raise false alerts. Set minimum durations in Value Search.
Hard-coding tag names
You end up rebuilding every line by hand. Build on the asset tree and swap.
cases.reported: About 10% OEE improvement on the target lines, twice the 5% first estimated. Lost time is found in real time; it is easy to tell a true bottleneck from a unit blocked upstream or downstream; about one month to build, then extended quickly to more products and lines.
cases.assumptions: The band width, the number of golden batches, the 12-hour trim and the tag names are not stated by Seeq. The source mentions visual dashboards but not email or SMS alerts.

cases.title: Upstream oil and gas well performance analysis
problem: Production engineers review hundreds to thousands of wells every day. The data sits in separate systems (Ignition SCADA, the PI historian, the asset database), and engineers calculate KPIs such as the Productivity Index by hand in spreadsheets.
That takes hundreds of hours and introduces errors. Poorly performing wells or faulty meters go unnoticed.
Data available: flow rate, reservoir and bottom-hole pressure, and Coriolis meter Drive Gain (a sign of entrained gas or a calibration problem).
cases.solution: Bring all sources into Seeq through its connectors and API, and arrange the wells in one asset tree so any calculation built once runs on every well. Calculate the Productivity Index continuously, flag meter upsets, add a prediction model to catch slow decline, and rank the worst wells automatically every morning.
cases.sourceNote: The Well Performance Trending page supplies the overall approach (API integration, custom asset tree, worksheet trending). The Productivity Index, Drive Gain, morning ranking script and time savings come from the related Seeq pages: Well Productivity Index, Field-Wide Analysis and Origin Energy.

steps.tool: Asset tree (Tree Builder, PI AF or Python SDK)
steps.inputs: SCADA tags and asset metadata
steps.settings: Field → Area → Well → Flow, Pressure, Drive Gain
steps.output: A standard structure for every well
steps.why: Everything built later scales to thousands of wells and compares like with like.

steps.inputs: Raw flow, pressure, Drive Gain
steps.settings: Remove communication dropouts, negative values and shut-in periods.
steps.why: Dropouts produce divide-by-zero errors and fake KPI spikes.

steps.inputs: Flow q, reservoir pressure, bottom-hole pressure
steps.settings: PI = flow ÷ (reservoir pressure − bottom-hole pressure)
steps.why: The main well-health KPI, now live instead of a spreadsheet.

steps.inputs: Drive Gain
steps.settings: is greater than 60%; maximum capsule 1 day
steps.why: Catches gas carry-over and calibration errors across the field.

steps.settings: Daily, in the field's local time zone
steps.why: Daily totals must match the local operating day.

steps.inputs: High Drive Gain, bounded by daily capsules
steps.settings: Total Duration in hours; timestamp at start
steps.why: A number you can sort and rank.

steps.inputs: Target: production; inputs such as choke position and tubing pressure; a good training period
steps.settings: Linear regression (OLS or ridge); keep inputs with p ≤ 0.05
steps.output: Expected production and the fit statistics (R²)
steps.why: The gap between expected and actual shows slow decline before it becomes a failure.

steps.inputs: Daily average PI; daily upset hours
steps.settings: Colour thresholds, e.g. PI green ≥ 1.0, red < 0.5; upset red > 2 h
steps.output: Colour table of well and meter health
steps.why: Shows at a glance where to look.

steps.inputs: Asset tree, worksheets
steps.settings: A scheduled script ranks wells by lowest PI and most upset hours and builds worksheets for the worst.
steps.why: Engineers start the day with the problem wells already listed.

example.caption: Well A-101, one day
rows: expected 800 bbl/day, so a 200 bbl/day shortfall

mistakes: Calculating on raw data
Zeros in the pressure difference blow up the PI. Clean first, and only calculate while the well is flowing.
Leaving daily windows in UTC
The day splits across two shifts and nothing matches the morning report. Set the site's time zone in Periodic Condition.
Hard-coding tag paths
Every new well means rebuilding. Build on the asset tree and swap.
cases.reported: The upstream use case page lists benefits but gives no figures. The related Well Productivity Index page reports about 500 engineering hours saved per 1,000 wells, 5 to 30 minutes per well per calculation, and fewer data-entry errors.
cases.assumptions: PI thresholds, the prediction training window, the script host and tag names are not stated by Seeq.

cases.title: Heat exchanger monitoring and end-of-cycle prediction
problem: In a refinery, crude oil is heated before distillation by a chain of heat exchangers called the preheat train. Other exchangers heat feeds before they go into reactors. As oil flows through, deposits build up on the tube walls. This is called fouling. It works like a blanket: less heat gets through, so the unit has to run at a lower rate, or be shut down and cleaned.

A major US oil and gas company cleaned its exchangers on a fixed calendar, every few months, whether they needed it or not. That wasted money. Engineers did the analysis by hand in spreadsheets and spent hours or days removing data from times when equipment was out of service.

Data available: temperatures and flow rates from the plant historian (OSIsoft PI, PHD or others); exchanger design data such as heat-transfer area, from the asset database or typed into Seeq; and fluid properties such as heat capacity, from a lookup or typed into Seeq.
cases.solution: Keep only the time the exchanger is running normally. From the temperatures and flows, calculate the heat-transfer coefficient U, which says how well heat is getting through. Fit a model of U falling over time, and read off the date when the predicted U drops to the lowest acceptable value. That date is the planned cleaning date. Comparing the current run with earlier runs shows when fouling sped up, and the model can be used to test whether a change in operation would make the run last longer.
cases.sourceNote: The use case page names Value Search, Custom Condition, Formula, Prediction and Journal. The smoothing step, the run-by-run overlay and the scorecard come from the Seeq Knowledge Base pages, not from this use case page. The ideas behind heat duty and LMTD come from the Wikipedia pages in the notebook.

steps.inputs: Crude flow signal from the historian
steps.settings: Flow is less than a minimum running rate (for example 10 m³/h). Turn on the option to ignore short gaps, so a brief dip does not split one run into two.
steps.output: A Downtime condition: one capsule for each stop
steps.why: U worked out while the exchanger is stopped is meaningless and would ruin the model.

steps.inputs: The trend of temperatures and flows
steps.settings: Draw capsules by hand around upsets, test runs or instrument faults that no simple rule catches.
steps.why: Some bad data has no clean rule, but still has to be left out.

steps.inputs: Downtime and Abnormal
steps.settings: Combine the two with Union, then take the inverse (everything outside them).
steps.why: All later maths and the model use only this time.

steps.inputs: Cold-side mass flow, heat capacity Cp, cold inlet and outlet temperatures
steps.settings: Give every input a unit. If the flow tag is volume per hour, multiply by density first to get mass flow.
steps.output: A heat duty signal Q, in kW
steps.why: Q is how much heat actually crossed the tubes.

steps.inputs: Hot inlet and outlet, cold inlet and outlet temperatures
steps.settings: Counter-current form. For a multi-pass shell-and-tube unit, multiply by a correction factor F from the design data.
steps.output: A log mean temperature difference signal, in K
steps.why: The driving temperature difference changes along the exchanger; LMTD is the fair average to use.

steps.inputs: Q, LMTD and the heat-transfer area A (a scalar)
steps.settings: U = Q ÷ (A × LMTD). Keep only values inside Running Clean.
steps.why: As fouling builds up, U falls. U is the health number for the exchanger.

steps.inputs: The U signal
steps.settings: Filter type: Seeq Agile Filter. Window about 24 hours to start.
steps.why: Small swings in rate and instrument noise hide the slow fouling trend.

steps.inputs: Smoothed U as the signal to model; a time signal (days since the last cleaning) as the input
steps.settings: Linear model to start, Ordinary Least Squares. Training window from the start of the current run to now. Turn on Limit to condition and pick Running Clean.
steps.output: A predicted U signal that carries on into the future
steps.why: This gives the fouling rate and lets you see where U is heading. In monitoring mode it updates as new data arrives.

steps.inputs: Predicted U and the minimum allowed U
steps.settings: Predicted U is less than or equal to the minimum (for example 300 W/m²·K). Search far enough ahead, such as one year.
steps.output: A capsule whose start is the predicted cleaning date
steps.why: This is the date maintenance and operations plan around, instead of a fixed calendar.

steps.tool: Capsule Time view, Scorecard Metric, Journal
steps.inputs: Smoothed U, one capsule per run between cleanings, the end-of-cycle date
steps.settings: Capsule Time overlays every run from its own start, so a steeper drop stands out. A Scorecard Metric shows current U, days left and the date. The Journal records each step for review.
steps.output: An overlay of runs, a status table and documented analysis
steps.why: Spotting a run that fouls faster points to its cause, such as a feed or rate change.

example.caption: Exchanger E-101, one day of clean running
example.note: All numbers are made up for teaching. Q is taken from the cold side; if the hot-side flow is also measured, both duties should agree within a few per cent.

mistakes: Mixing up units
Volume flow (m³/h) in the heat duty formula, or kJ mixed with W, gives answers wrong by factors of 1,000 or 3,600. Give every tag and scalar a unit and convert volume flow to mass flow first.
Training the model on shutdown data
When the exchanger stops, the temperatures collapse and U spikes to zero or below, which drags the fitted line. Build Running Clean first and use Limit to condition in Prediction.
Training across several cleanings
U jumps back up after each cleaning, so a line fitted across runs averages different fouling rates and gives a wrong date. Start the training window at the most recent cleaning.
cases.reported: Lower production loss, worth roughly $10,000 a year. Maintenance moved from a fixed calendar to a risk-based plan. Fewer unplanned rate cuts caused by heat-transfer limits, avoiding the loss of millions of dollars in crude and intermediate processing margin. Weeks of spreadsheet work removed, and the analysis was scaled to other exchangers and other sites. The refinery expects to save millions of dollars a year from better turnaround planning (an expectation, not a measured result).
cases.assumptions: Seeq does not give tag names, the downtime flow limit, the minimum allowed U, the smoothing window, the model type or training window, or whether an LMTD correction factor was used. None of the Formula expressions come from the use case page. It does not say how many exchangers or sites were included, or whether the $10,000 a year is per exchanger or in total.

cases.title: Value-based maintenance: RWE's gas turbine fleet
problem: RWE runs Europe's second-largest fleet of gas turbines: over 31 power plants and 15.7 GW of gas-fired capacity. Its leaders made reliability the top goal. Fixing things after they break, or servicing them on a calendar, was no longer good enough.

Failures are expensive. A leaking stop ratio valve (the valve that shuts off fuel gas to the turbine) caused forced shutdowns costing about £1.3m each in lost production. Igniters failed during startups, high-temperature parts wore out without good tracking, and blocked air filters let water into the compressor. There were hundreds of possible failure modes and no data-based way to decide which to fix first.
Data available: process data in PI, maintenance records in SAP and local logs, all kept in separate places.
cases.solution: Value-based maintenance. For each failure mode, Seeq turns raw sensor data into a simple indicator of how healthy the part is. RWE sends these indicators to its own reliability platform, MARA, which combines them with how likely and how costly each failure is into a health score. The fleet's risks are then ranked, so engineers work on the problems worth the most money first. This walkthrough builds one example: checking the stop ratio valve for leaks during each startup and rundown test.
cases.sourceNote: The RWE page names the failure modes, the health score idea, MARA and the results, but it does not say how any indicator is calculated. The build steps (speed and valve-command searches, the pressure ratio, peak per test) were worked out by the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base pages and the related Valve Health Diagnostics page. Treat them as one sensible way to build it, not RWE's exact method.

steps.inputs: Turbine speed (or the unit's start sequence tag)
steps.settings: Speed between a low value (for example 10 rpm) and full speed. Set a maximum capsule duration, such as 4 hours, so a stuck signal cannot make a capsule months long.
steps.output: A Startup/Rundown condition: one capsule per event
steps.why: The valve can only be leak-tested when it is shut while fuel gas pressure is present, which happens during these tests.

steps.n: Find when the valve is commanded shut
steps.inputs: Stop ratio valve position command
steps.settings: Command is less than or equal to 0 %.
steps.why: Pressure behind an open valve is normal; only a shut valve shows a leak.

steps.inputs: Startup/Rundown and SRV Closed
steps.settings: Intersection (A and B).
steps.output: An SRV Leak Test Window condition
steps.why: Every later number is worked out only inside this window.

steps.inputs: Gas pressure upstream and downstream of the valve
steps.settings: Downstream pressure as a percentage of upstream pressure. A tight valve keeps the downstream side near zero.
steps.why: Dividing by the supply pressure makes tests comparable even when the supply pressure changes.

steps.inputs: Leakage Ratio, bounded by the test window
steps.settings: Statistic: Maximum. Timestamp at the end of the capsule. Interpolation: Step or Discrete, not Linear.
steps.output: A Peak Leakage per Test signal: one point per startup or rundown
steps.why: Turns a fast-changing signal into one trackable number per event, ready to export.

steps.inputs: Leakage Ratio and the test windows
steps.settings: Line up every test from its own start and overlay them.
steps.why: A curve that rises a bit higher each time shows the valve seat wearing before any limit trips.

steps.inputs: Peak Leakage per Test
steps.settings: Condition metric over the test windows; thresholds such as green below 5 %, yellow 5 to 15 %, red above 15 %.
steps.output: A colour-coded table per valve and turbine
steps.why: Engineers see at a glance which valves need attention.

steps.inputs: The peak leakage indicator from every turbine
steps.settings: RWE sends Seeq indicators to MARA through its data feeds; the page does not say how. MARA adds likelihood, cost and history.
steps.output: A fleet-wide health score that ranks failure modes
steps.why: Puts the money and the engineering together, so the most valuable fixes come first.

example.caption: One GT26 turbine, three startups (upstream gas pressure 50 bar)
example.note: All numbers except the £1.3m are made up for teaching, including the trip chances and the simple score (100 minus the trip chance in %). RWE's real scoring method is not published.

mistakes: Calculating over all running time
With fuel flowing the downstream pressure is high anyway, so the indicator is meaningless. Calculate only inside the test window.
Linear interpolation between tests
Tests can be weeks apart; a straight line invents values in between. Use Step or Discrete in Signal from Condition and stamp each value at the end of the test.
No maximum capsule duration
A stuck valve or speed signal can create one capsule lasting months, which slows everything and gives wrong peaks. Always set a sensible maximum, such as 4 hours.
cases.reported: Stop ratio valve monitoring during startup and rundown tests prevented two major breakdowns since 2021, each outage costing about £1.3m (so roughly £2.6m avoided in total). Igniter monitoring reduced failed starts; creep life is now tracked in real time instead of by manual analysis; filter replacement dates are predicted from water ingress risk. Across the programme: hundreds of failure models in use, 70+ active Seeq data feeds into MARA, more than 50% of Seeq users are trained experts who build models, and a new RIEO (Reliability, Integrity, Efficiency, Optimization) team. Seeq is used on 12+ GT26 units.
cases.assumptions: The RWE page does not give the leakage formula, the sensors used, how startup windows are found, the scorecard limits, how indicators reach MARA, or how the health score is calculated. Tag names, the 4-hour limit and all thresholds here are placeholders.

cases.title: Uniper: boiler wall temperature excursions in coal plants
problem: Uniper is a European energy company with 7,000 employees in more than 40 countries and a 22.4 GW generation portfolio. Its coal and gas plants keep the grid stable while Europe moves away from coal, so they must be reliable and efficient. The Uniper page covers two cases: gas turbine efficiency and boiler tube failures in coal plants. This walkthrough builds the second.

In a coal-fired boiler, the furnace walls are made of water-filled tubes. If parts of the wall run hotter than their design limit, the metal slowly stretches and thins (this is called creep) until a tube leaks. A tube leak forces a large unit of 1,100+ MW to shut down for days, losing revenue just when conventional power is needed most.
Data available: more than 450 wall temperature sensors on each unit. Excel could not handle that much data, so excursions were hard to find, measure or predict.
cases.solution: Exception-based monitoring. Clean the temperature signals, mark every time a sensor goes above its design limit while the boiler is running, and add up how long and how hot each excursion was. Roll the totals into a colour table so engineers see which wall zones are under the most stress, and plan inspections and tube work for those zones. Seeq Data Lab (Python) repeats the same logic across all 450+ sensors.
cases.sourceNote: The Uniper page says Seeq Workbench and Data Lab were used, with capsule and value search logic to categorise excursions against boiler design parameters. It does not give the limit, the summary period or the scorecard settings; those come from the notebook, the Seeq Knowledge Base pages and the Wikipedia pages on boilers and creep.

steps.inputs: Raw wall thermocouple signals
steps.settings: Drop impossible readings (for example a sensor reporting -999) and apply light smoothing, such as an Agile Filter over about 1 minute.
steps.why: Thermocouples in a hot furnace glitch often; without cleaning, every glitch looks like an excursion.

steps.n: Find when the boiler is running
steps.inputs: Unit load (MW) or fuel firing signal
steps.settings: Load is greater than a minimum, for example 100 MW.
steps.why: Startups, cool-downs and outages have their own temperature swings that are not normal-operation stress.

steps.inputs: Each clean temperature signal
steps.settings: Temperature is greater than the design limit (for example 550 °C), lasting at least 10 seconds; maximum capsule 1 day.
steps.why: Turns hours of trend data into a list of events you can count.

steps.inputs: Excursion and Boiler Running
steps.settings: Intersection (A and B).
steps.why: Removes false alarms from startups and shutdowns.

steps.inputs: None
steps.settings: Weekly, in the plant's local time zone.
steps.why: Gives a fixed period to add up stress over, so weeks and sensors can be compared.

steps.n: Add up hours and peak temperature
steps.inputs: Operating Excursion (for hours) and clean temperature (for the peak), bounded by the weekly capsules
steps.settings: Statistics: Total Duration of excursions, and Maximum temperature. Timestamp at the start of the week. Step interpolation.
steps.output: Two weekly signals per sensor: hours above the limit, and peak temperature
steps.why: Creep damage grows with both how long and how far the metal is over its limit.

steps.inputs: Weekly excursion hours and peak temperature
steps.settings: Thresholds such as green below 1 h a week, yellow 1 to 5 h, red above 5 h or peak above 580 °C.
steps.output: A colour table of every sensor and zone
steps.why: Shows the bad actors among 450+ sensors at a glance.

steps.inputs: Operating Excursion and the temperatures
steps.settings: Overlay every excursion from its own start; show some data before and after each one.
steps.why: Patterns just before the excursions, such as load swings or sootblowing, point to the cause.

steps.inputs: The worksheet logic and the sensor list
steps.settings: Python script repeats the same steps for all 450+ sensors and every unit.
steps.why: Nobody can build 450 searches by hand; the page says Data Lab did these calculations.

example.caption: Boiler wall zone 3, four sensors, one week (168 h, boiler running 150 h, limit 550 °C)
rows: 2 excursions found; 1 was during startup and is removed (step 4); 0.75 h above the limit, peak 562 °C → green
4 excursions, 3.20 h, peak 574 °C → yellow (1 to 5 h)
7 found, 1 during startup removed, so 6 excursions; 6.80 h, peak 591 °C → red (over 5 h and over 580 °C)
example.note: All numbers are made up for teaching. TC-304 is the bad actor: plan a wall-thickness check at that spot in the next outage.

mistakes: Not filtering for running time
Startup and cool-down spikes create false excursions and inflate the stress numbers. Always intersect with Boiler Running.
No minimum duration or cleaning
A sensor flickering around 550 °C makes hundreds of one-second capsules. Clean the signal first and require the excursion to last, for example, 10 seconds.
Wrong timestamp or interpolation for weekly totals
End or middle timestamps put the week's value in the wrong place, and Linear draws fake slopes between weeks. Use Start and Step.
cases.reported: A fleet-wide view of boiler wall stress, better able to manage tube failure risk; insight into where leaks are most likely to occur; condition-based maintenance that reduces unplanned unavailability; a move from reactive, site-level monitoring to central risk management. Across both Uniper cases: significant time savings from reusable templates and analytics open to more people than a few site engineers. The page gives no money or hours figures.
cases.assumptions: The Uniper page does not name the historian, the temperature limit, the sensors per zone, a weekly summary period, the scorecard limits or the minimum excursion length. Those here are placeholders. It also does not give the creep equations used, if any.

cases.title: Minimize vented steam in a dual boiler system
problem: Many plants make their steam with two boilers. A boiler cannot turn down below a minimum firing rate. In warm months the plant needs less steam, so with both boilers at minimum they still make more steam than is used, and the extra is vented to the air.

Vented steam is wasted fuel, money and CO2. Running on one boiler would stop the venting, but if that single boiler trips, the plant can lose production. Managers need numbers to weigh the saving against that risk.
Data available: boiler firing rates or steam flows, vent flow or vent valve position, and outside air temperature, from the plant historian. The Seeq page does not name the historian or the tags.
cases.solution: Find the times when both boilers sit at minimum firing and steam is still being vented, and add up the vented steam over a year to get its cost. Then use history to estimate how often a single boiler would trip, and multiply by what a trip costs (probability × financial consequence). If the steam saving is clearly bigger than the risk, idle one boiler in warm weather.
cases.sourceNote: The use case page gives the idea (conditions for minimum firing with venting, yearly steam savings, trip risk as probability × consequence) and the result. The exact tools, settings and formulas below come from the notebook and the Seeq Knowledge Base pages; the expected-value idea is from Wikipedia.

steps.n: Find both boilers at minimum firing
steps.inputs: Boiler 1 and Boiler 2 firing rates
steps.settings: One Value Search per boiler: firing rate less than or equal to its minimum (for example 20 %). Combine with Intersection (both at once). Ignore short gaps so small wobbles don't split events.

cases.title: Increase capacity through optimal product transition scheduling
problem: One chemical reactor can make many different products (grades) by changing its conditions. Switching from one grade to the next is called a transition. During a transition the reactor makes material that is in spec for neither product. This off-spec material sells at a much lower margin, and the transition uses up reactor hours.

Engineers can cut these losses by choosing a better order and length for the production cycle. But that needs to know, for every type of transition, how long it takes and how much off-spec it makes, which means digging through years of data.
Data available: process data (set points, grade code, flows, temperatures) from AspenTech IP21, Honeywell PHD or AVEVA PI; quality results from the lab system (LIMS).
cases.solution: Find every past transition automatically from the step changes in set points or the grade code. Use the lab results to set the real start (Product A goes out of spec) and end (Product B comes into spec). Label each transition with its from-grade and to-grade, measure its time and off-spec amount, and average these by transition type. Then rebuild the production cycle so it uses the quickest, cheapest transitions.
cases.sourceNote: Every tool on this list is named on the use case page. The exact settings and Formula expressions come from the notebook and the Seeq Knowledge Base. The $850k and railcar figures sometimes quoted with this case belong to the related Chemical Reactor Product Transition Optimization page, not this one.

steps.inputs: Set points, feed rate and other process signals
steps.settings: Remove outliers and downtime; smooth noisy signals, for example with an Agile Filter.
steps.why: The next step takes a rate of change, which makes noise much worse; cleaning first prevents false transitions.

steps.inputs: Grade code or key controller set points
steps.settings: Take the derivative (rate of change).
steps.output: A rate-of-change signal that spikes when a set point steps
steps.why: A step change becomes a clear peak, which is easy to search for.

steps.inputs: The rate-of-change signal
steps.settings: Absolute value is greater than a small threshold; maximum capsule duration such as 1 day.
steps.output: A Transition condition: one capsule per transition
steps.why: Finds every transition in years of data without anyone scrolling through trends.

steps.n: Label the from and to grade
steps.inputs: Transition capsules and the grade code
steps.settings: Store the grade at the start and at the end of each capsule as capsule properties.
steps.why: Lets you group and compare like transitions, even years apart.

steps.n: Set the real start and end from quality
steps.inputs: Transition capsules and LIMS quality results
steps.settings: Start when the lab result leaves Product A's spec; end when it enters Product B's spec.
steps.output: Transition capsules that match the actual off-spec time
steps.why: The set point changes in a second, but the reactor takes hours to respond; only the quality data shows the true loss window.

steps.inputs: Production rate, bounded by the transition capsules
steps.settings: Statistic: Duration (hours) for time, Totalized for off-spec amount. Timestamp at start.
steps.output: Hours and off-spec tonnes for every transition
steps.why: Turns each window into numbers you can compare.

steps.inputs: Hours and off-spec per transition, grouped by the from/to labels
steps.settings: Statistics: average, minimum and maximum per transition type.
steps.output: A table of transition types ranked by time and off-spec
steps.why: Shows which transitions are cheap and which are expensive.

steps.inputs: The ranked transition table
steps.settings: Record each trial production order in the Journal; summarise the best one in an Organizer Topic.
steps.output: A recommended production order, and a report
steps.why: The page says the Topic made the case to the business team and is used at monthly reconciliation meetings to compare actual against planned transition losses.

mistakes: Using the set point change as the transition
Reactors lag, so the real off-spec period starts and ends later. Trim the capsules with the lab quality data.
Taking a derivative of raw data
Differentiation amplifies noise into false spikes and many tiny capsules. Smooth first.
No downtime filter or maximum capsule length
Shutdowns can create fake multi-day transitions. Remove downtime and set a maximum duration in Value Search.
cases.reported: The analysis shows how much off-spec material and how many reactor hours each transition type uses, so engineers can build a production cycle around the best transitions. A commodity polymer maker reported a significant cut in transition time, making its average production campaign 5% shorter and letting it run above nameplate capacity in the freed reactor hours.

cases.title: Chemical reactor product transition optimization (golden transition profile)
problem: A chemical reactor can make different products by changing its conditions. Switching from Product A to Product B makes material that meets neither specification. This off-spec or wide-spec material is sold at a much lower margin, so plants want transitions that are short and make little off-spec.

Improving transitions means digging through years of data: finding each transition, overlaying many reactor and lab values, working out exact start and end times and calculating KPIs. With spreadsheets and historian trend tools that cannot be done at scale.
Data available: process data from AspenTech IP21, Honeywell PHD or OSIsoft PI; quality data from the lab system (LIMS).
cases.solution: Find every transition automatically, set its real start and end from the lab results, and label it with its from-grade and to-grade. Then look at one transition type at a time (for example A → B), pick the past run that was fastest with the least off-spec, and build a reference profile (a 'golden' curve) of the key reactor values from it. Operators follow that curve as a target during the next A → B transition.
cases.sourceNote: The tools are the ones named on the page (Formula derivatives, Value Search, Formula to map grades and filter, Reference Profile, Journal, Organizer Topic). Capsule Time, Signal from Condition and the exact settings come from the notebook and the Seeq Knowledge Base.

steps.inputs: Raw reactor signals
steps.settings: Remove outliers and downtime; smooth with an Agile Filter.
steps.why: Noise makes false transitions in the next steps.

steps.inputs: Grade code or controller set points
steps.settings: Take the derivative; search where its absolute value is above a small threshold for at least 10 seconds; maximum capsule 1 day.
steps.why: Every step change in grade or set point marks a transition.

steps.inputs: Lab quality result (for example melt flow index) and the spec limits of both grades
steps.settings: Start when quality leaves Product A's spec; end when it enters Product B's spec. Combine with the transition capsules.
steps.why: The reactor lags behind the set point; only the lab data shows the true loss window.

steps.n: Label and filter one transition type
steps.inputs: Off-spec transitions and the grade code
steps.settings: Add From Grade and To Grade as capsule properties, then keep only A → B.
steps.why: Different grade pairs behave differently; compare like with like.

steps.inputs: Production rate, bounded by A → B Transitions
steps.settings: Duration (hours) and Totalized off-spec tonnes per capsule.
steps.output: Hours and off-spec tonnes for every A → B run
steps.why: Ranks the runs so the best one can be picked.

steps.inputs: The A → B runs, key reactor signals, the per-run KPIs
steps.settings: Overlay all runs from their own start; sort by off-spec and duration; select the best run (or the best few).
steps.why: The best real run is a target the plant has already proved it can hit.

steps.inputs: Key reactor signal (for example temperature), the golden capsule(s), gridding period such as 1 minute
steps.settings: Reference statistic: Average. For ± standard deviation bands you need several good runs; with a single run, add fixed offsets in Formula instead. Apply the profile to future A → B transitions.
steps.output: A golden curve (and limits) shown against every new transition
steps.why: Operators can see early if a live transition is falling behind and correct it.

steps.inputs: Worksheets per transition type, results
steps.settings: Journal links for each grade pair so engineers can reopen the right view before a transition; a Topic comparing transitions with the golden profile, before and after.
steps.output: Ready-made views and a results report
steps.why: The page says engineers use these before each transition and to show the step change in off-spec.

example.caption: Grade A → B, five past runs and one new run (90 t per railcar, $150/t margin loss)
rows: New run following the golden profile
Saved per year at 2 transitions a month
example.note: All numbers are made up for teaching. The real case reports 3 to 5 railcars saved per transition.

mistakes: Mixing all transition types together
A → B and B → C behave differently, so a combined average is meaningless. Label each capsule with its grades and filter to one type.
Using only set point changes for start and end
The reactor lags, so off-spec time and tonnes are underestimated. Use the lab results to set the window.
Expecting standard deviation bands from one run
A single capsule has no spread. Use several good runs for statistical bands, or fixed offsets around one golden run.
cases.reported: Engineers use the reference profile as the target for the next transition. A specialty polyethylene unit cut transition off-spec by 5 railcars compared with past transitions. Repeating the analysis for its other upcoming transitions gave repeatable savings of 3 to 5 railcars of off-spec per transition. For one production line with about 2 transitions a month, this saved an estimated $850k per year in margin lost to downgrades.
cases.assumptions: The page does not give tag names, the quality property or spec limits, thresholds, the gridding period, how many runs the profile used, the railcar size or the margin per tonne.

cases.title: Weather-based load predictions
problem: How much electricity homes and businesses use depends strongly on the weather: hot days mean air conditioning, cold days mean heating. Utilities want to use weather forecasts to predict demand, but weather has been an under-used input to their load forecasts.

Large service areas have several weather stations, and combining them explains more of the load. The spread of the load data, the geography of the area and the number and location of stations all affect how good a forecast can be.
Data available: load measurements from the utility's systems, NOAA and local weather forecasts, and future (forecast) data stored in OSIsoft PI (OSIsoft Future Data), all brought together in Seeq.
cases.solution: Learn the link between weather and load from the past, then apply it to the weather forecast to predict future load. Mark which data is history (fixed) and which is forecast (changes every update). Train a regression model in Seeq's Prediction tool on history, run it on the forecast, and show the model's error as a band that widens further out. Build it once and repeat it for every zone, customer class and critical asset with an asset tree.
cases.sourceNote: The page names Seeq Cortex for the data, the Prediction tool, model error on the forecast, capsules for history versus future, the asset tree and the Treemap view. Settings and Formula expressions come from the notebook and the Seeq Knowledge Base; the comparison with substation ratings is borrowed from the related Energy Storage page.

steps.inputs: Load, temperature and humidity signals
steps.settings: Remove gaps, outliers and outages; smooth the load lightly, for example a low-pass filter over 15 minutes.
steps.why: Spikes and gaps distort the regression.

steps.inputs: Clean load and the weather forecast
steps.settings: One condition for the past, where both load and weather are measured; one for the future, where only forecast weather exists.
steps.why: The page says capsules for historical and future states keep calculations fast and stop the model training on data that will change.

steps.inputs: Target: clean load. Inputs: temperature and humidity (from one or more stations).
steps.settings: Linear regression, Ordinary Least Squares (or Ridge if inputs move together); try a polynomial term for the curved air-conditioning effect; training window inside History; keep only inputs with p-value ≤ 0.05.
steps.output: A fitted model with coefficients and R², and a modelled load signal
steps.why: Measures how much load changes per degree and per % humidity.

steps.inputs: The fitted model and the NOAA / Future Data weather forecast
steps.settings: Evaluate the model over the Forecast condition using forecast temperatures.
steps.output: A predicted load signal into the future
steps.why: This is the forecast operators act on.

steps.inputs: Predicted load and the model's standard error
steps.settings: Upper and lower lines at the prediction ± a margin; widen the margin further out in time.
steps.output: An error band around the forecast
steps.why: The page says error is built into the forecast so people see the range of possible outcomes.

steps.inputs: Predicted peak load and each substation's rating
steps.settings: Daily maximum; colours such as green below 80 % of rating, yellow 80 to 100 %, red above 100 %.
steps.output: A colour table of forecast loading
steps.why: Shows which circuits or substations are heading for trouble.

steps.inputs: Zones, customer classes and critical assets with their load and weather signals
steps.settings: Build the worksheet once and swap assets; show forecast risk in a Treemap.
steps.output: The same forecast for every zone, with hot spots highlighted
steps.why: The page says the same analytics are applied across locations, customer classes and assets.

rows: Plan demand response or other mitigation before the afternoon peak

Gaps, outages or forecast periods in the training window give a wrong model. Train only inside the History condition on clean data.
Forgetting to feed in the forecast
A model trained on measured temperature cannot predict ahead unless you run it on the forecast temperature signal.
Building one worksheet per substation by hand
It cannot be maintained. Build on one template asset and use the asset tree to copy it everywhere.

cases.title: Methane plume detection
problem: Oil and gas operators find it hard to pinpoint methane leaks. Satellites can measure methane, but only about once a day, and that data sits apart from weather and plant process data.
So it is hard to measure leak events afterwards, almost impossible to spot them while they happen, and harder still to see one coming and prevent it.
Data available: satellite methane data, weather data through Seeq's NOAA weather connector, and the plant's own process data.
cases.solution: Put satellite, weather and process data side by side in Seeq. Use the satellite reading to flag that an event happened. Use the wind to see how the plume spread and which direction it came from. Then use process data to find the source and to measure when the event started and stopped and how much methane was released.
cases.sourceNote: The page names Value Search, Signal from Condition and Formula, plus filters and capsules for data wrangling. The wind-direction step, the padding of the daily satellite sample and the settings come from the notebook and the Seeq Knowledge Base; dispersion ideas come from Wikipedia.

steps.inputs: Satellite methane, NOAA wind speed and direction, process tags
steps.settings: Remove invalid values and dropouts; light smoothing on noisy tags.
steps.why: Bad points cause false alarms and wrong totals later.

steps.inputs: Satellite methane reading
steps.settings: Reading is greater than the background by a set amount (for example 50 ppb above about 1,900 ppb). Maximum capsule 1 day.
steps.why: The once-a-day reading is the first warning that something happened.

steps.inputs: Satellite Event condition
steps.settings: A single daily sample makes a capsule with almost no length. Pad it, for example 12 hours either side, so it overlaps the continuous weather and process data.
steps.why: Without padding nothing else can be compared with the event.

steps.n: Read the wind during the window
steps.inputs: Wind direction and speed, bounded by Candidate Window
steps.settings: Statistic: Average. Timestamp at start.
steps.output: Average wind direction and speed for each event
steps.why: The plume drifts downwind, so the source lies upwind. This narrows down which unit to look at.

steps.inputs: Tags on the upwind units (relief valve position, flare flow, pressures)
steps.settings: For example relief valve open, or flare flow above a limit.
steps.output: A Process Upset condition per candidate unit
steps.why: Process data is continuous, so it shows the real start and end of the release, not just the moment the satellite passed.

steps.inputs: Process Upset and Candidate Window
steps.settings: Intersection (both at the same time).
steps.output: A Confirmed Leak condition with real start and end times
steps.why: Links the satellite detection to one piece of equipment.

steps.inputs: Leak rate signal (measured or modelled), bounded by Confirmed Leak
steps.settings: Statistics: Duration (hours) and Totalized mass (kg).
steps.output: Event duration and methane emitted for each event
steps.why: These are the numbers needed for reporting and for judging how bad the event was.

steps.inputs: Process signals around each Confirmed Leak
steps.settings: Overlay events from their start, showing some time before each one.
steps.why: Repeating patterns before events become early warning signs, so future events can be prevented.

example.caption: One site, one day
rows: from 225° (south-west) at 4.2 m/s → look at units to the south-west
example.note: All numbers are made up for teaching.

mistakes: Treating the satellite pass time as the leak time
The satellite sees one moment a day. Use process data to find when the release really started and stopped.
Working on raw, noisy data
Spikes and dropouts give false events and wrong totals. Clean first.
Leaving the daily sample as a zero-length capsule
It will not overlap anything. Pad the satellite event into a window, for example 12 hours either side.
cases.reported: Overlaying process, weather and satellite data gives better insight into emission events: how long they lasted, how much was emitted and how the plume spread. This helps link process events to methane releases, spot events as they happen so they can be mitigated, and find early signs that an event is about to happen so it can be prevented. The page gives no figures.

cases.title: Pipeline drag reducing agent (DRA) optimization
problem: Pipeline operators inject a drag reducing agent (DRA), a chemical that cuts friction in the pipe, so the product keeps its required properties as it travels down the line. The chemical is expensive, so injecting it where it is not needed wastes money.
Working out the best injection with spreadsheets is slow and does not work well.
Data available: process data (flows, pressures along each segment, DRA injection) from historians such as OSIsoft PI.
cases.solution: Measure the hydraulic performance of every pipeline segment continuously, using only data inside a chosen flow rate range. Compare segments to find bottlenecks and to see where DRA helps most. Put DRA where it is needed and cut it where it is not, while making sure the product at the end of the line stays on spec. A flow rate range the user enters lets the tool anticipate DRA needs for forecast rates.
cases.sourceNote: The page lists Value Search, Formula, Histogram, Scorecard and an Organizer Topic. The pressure-drop-per-km measure and percent drag reduction come from the notebook and the Wikipedia pages (Darcy–Weisbach, drag reducing agent). The page does not name the Prediction tool; the last step is one way to do the forecasting it describes.

steps.inputs: Pipeline flow rate
steps.settings: Flow is between a low and a high limit (for example 200 to 500 m³/h); maximum capsule 1 day; ignore short gaps.
steps.why: The page removes periods outside the selected flow range; comparing segments at very different flows would be unfair.

steps.n: Pressure drop per km for each segment
steps.inputs: Segment inlet and outlet pressure, segment length (scalar)
steps.settings: (inlet − outlet) ÷ length. Give the length a unit.
steps.why: Puts segments of different lengths on the same scale; a high value means more friction.

steps.inputs: DRA injection rate and Flow In Range
steps.settings: DRA On: injection above zero, intersected with Flow In Range. DRA Off: injection zero, also inside Flow In Range.
steps.output: DRA On and DRA Off conditions per segment
steps.why: You need a fair baseline without DRA to see what the chemical actually does.

steps.inputs: Pressure drop per km averaged over DRA On and over DRA Off
steps.settings: Condition scorecard, statistic Average; then % reduction = (off − on) ÷ off × 100.
steps.why: Shows where each litre of DRA does the most good.

steps.inputs: Pressure drop per km, by segment
steps.settings: Bins of pressure drop; statistic Count or Average.
steps.output: Distribution of hydraulic performance per segment
steps.why: Shows which segments are consistent and which swing, pointing to bottlenecks.

steps.inputs: Pressure drop, drag reduction and DRA cost per segment
steps.settings: Colour thresholds, for example red for a bottleneck segment, green where DRA works well.
steps.output: A colour table of every segment
steps.why: Makes the reallocation decision obvious.

steps.inputs: Historical DRA rate against flow, and the forecast flow
steps.settings: Fit DRA need as a function of flow inside the chosen range, then evaluate at the forecast flow.
steps.output: Expected DRA need at the planned rate
steps.why: The page says users enter a flow range to anticipate DRA needs based on forecast rates.

steps.inputs: Scorecards and histograms per segment and pipeline
steps.settings: One section per pipeline, one row per segment.
steps.why: The page says an Organizer Topic summarises results for each segment in each pipeline.

Segment B with DRA at 20 ppm

mistakes: Averaging over shutdowns and odd flows
Zero-flow and low-flow periods wreck the averages. Always bound calculations by Flow In Range.
Numbers without units
Pressures, lengths and flows without units can give silent unit errors. Give every tag and scalar a unit.
Using a fixed-time scorecard for event periods
A continuous (clock-based) metric mixes DRA-on and DRA-off time. Use a condition metric bounded by DRA On or DRA Off.

This greatly reduces yearly spending on the DRA chemical, saving pipeline operators major operating costs that were unnecessary. The page gives no figures.

cases.title: Biopharma fill weight analytics and bad batch prediction
problem: In biopharma manufacturing, each vial must hold the right fill weight. Often the plant only learns at the end of a batch that product is over or under weight, and then the batch is scrapped or capacity is lost. Fill weights must stay consistent across products, doses, batches and time.

Predicting a 'bad batch' from many operating conditions at once (multivariate analysis) is hard, and doing near real-time monitoring, quality prediction and root cause analysis in spreadsheets is slow. Spreadsheets also make it hard to share work across teams and sites, and to bring several data sources together.
Data available: process data in OSIsoft PI with PI Asset Framework, and Amazon Redshift (with MES data planned).
cases.solution: Run Seeq on AWS so engineers and operators can reach near real-time data from anywhere. Mark each filling run, track fill weight against expected limits during the run, and build a model that predicts the batch result from live operating conditions. Notify operators when a bad batch is coming so they can act early. Build the analysis on one fill line and copy it to hundreds of assets through PI Asset Framework.
cases.sourceNote: The page describes the goals, AWS, notifications and PI AF scaling, but names no specific Seeq tools and gives no numbers. The build steps come from the notebook, the Seeq Knowledge Base and the related Batch Quality Prediction and SPC pages. The 'millions of dollars saved' sometimes quoted belongs to the Batch Quality Prediction page, not this one.

steps.inputs: Line state or batch tag
steps.settings: State equals 'FILLING'; maximum capsule 12 hours; ignore short gaps.
steps.output: A Filling condition, one capsule per run
steps.why: Leaves out idle time, cleaning and startups, which would skew everything else.

steps.inputs: Fill weight and key process signals, bounded by Filling
steps.settings: Average (and standard deviation) per batch; timestamp at start; step interpolation.
steps.output: One value per batch for fill weight and each process input
steps.why: Lets you compare batches and train a model on batch-level numbers.

steps.inputs: Fill weight signal, known good batches
steps.settings: Average with ±3 standard deviation limits; gridding about 1 to 5 minutes; apply to new batches.
steps.output: Upper and lower limits that follow the batch
steps.why: Shows drift during the run instead of at the end. These are control limits; keep the product specification limits separate.

steps.inputs: Target: final fill weight (or quality result). Inputs: dosing pump pressure, line speed, temperature and similar.
steps.settings: Training window of good representative batches; Limit to condition = Filling; OLS, or PCA if inputs move together; set a refresh rate so the model is not refitted constantly.
steps.why: Warns while the batch is still running, before lab results arrive.

steps.inputs: Predicted fill weight and its limits
steps.settings: Predicted value outside the limits for at least 30 seconds.
steps.why: Turns the prediction into a clear event.

steps.inputs: Bad Batch Warning
steps.settings: Send an alert to operators and engineers when a capsule starts; show live status on a shared dashboard.
steps.why: The page's goal is to notify operators so they can step in before the batch is lost.

steps.inputs: The worksheet built on one fill line
steps.settings: Map the inputs to the PI AF hierarchy and swap to each line.
steps.output: The same analysis on every line and site
steps.why: The page says insights built on one asset or batch scale quickly to hundreds of assets with PI AF.

mistakes: Training on idle and cleaning time
Downtime and cleaning cycles skew the model and the limits. Use the Filling condition everywhere, including Limit to condition in Prediction.
Refitting the model constantly
Recalculating a multivariate model on every data point slows worksheets. Set a refresh rate in Prediction.

cases.title: Overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) across a site
problem: Overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) shows how much of a plant's possible output it really makes. Knowing OEE for every unit on a site helps find bottlenecks and raise production.

But OEE is hard to calculate the same way, and at scale, across many similar and different units, so visibility is poor and improvement is slow. This site measured OEE only by uptime, which hid long periods when units were running but held back by some constraint.

cases.title: Energy storage capital expense optimization (where to put batteries)
problem: Each substation in a transmission and distribution (T&D) network has several transformers feeding local circuits. A substation's capacity is usually the sum of its transformer ratings, and utilities must report to regulators when load goes over capacity. So a utility can compare total MVA load with the total normal rating and the 24-hour emergency rating.

To avoid overloads, utilities install batteries. Batteries are expensive, so the location matters. The choice depends on whether the transformers can serve today's peak, whether the others can carry the whole station if one fails, asset health, outage impact, forecast demand and battery cost.
Data available: load data in PI; transformer capacity ratings in a SQL database.
cases.solution: Add up the transformer loads, smooth them, and compare them with the normal and emergency ratings. Ask 'what if one transformer had failed?' by checking whether the remaining transformer could have carried the whole load. Measure how often and how long limits would be exceeded, and repeat the same analysis for every substation with asset swapping, so batteries go where the risk of overload is highest.

cases.title: True transformer age for replacement
problem: Deciding when to replace a substation power transformer is hard. Manufacturers usually call 40 years the end of life, but a lightly loaded transformer may not reach a true age of 40 until its 60th or 70th year in service.

Working out how loading above the nameplate rating has aged a transformer over many years is very difficult without the right analytics, so it is almost impossible to know its true age and the right time to replace it.
Data available: load, temperature and oil/gas analysis data in PI; equipment heat-run properties (from factory tests) in a SQL database.
cases.solution: Use the IEEE C57.91-2011 standard, which gives an aging acceleration factor for a given load and temperature and the percent loss of life of the insulation. In Seeq, combine live temperature and load data with each transformer's nameplate and heat-run data, calculate how fast it is ageing at every moment, add that up over time to get its true age, and compare transformers across the fleet.
cases.sourceNote: The page names IEEE C57.91-2011, PI and SQL data, and the tools Formula, Value Search, Scatterplot, Scorecard, asset swapping and Treemap. The hot-spot and ageing equations are the standard IEEE/Arrhenius forms added by the notebook (with the Wikipedia Arrhenius page); the page does not print them.

steps.inputs: Load, top-oil and ambient temperature (PI); rated load, rated hot-spot rise and winding exponent (SQL)
steps.settings: Attach each transformer's signals and nameplate values to its node in the asset tree.

steps.inputs: Top-oil temperature, load ÷ rated load, rated hot-spot rise, exponent m
steps.settings: Hot-spot = top-oil + rated rise × (load ratio)^m (or use a measured winding temperature if there is one).
steps.why: The insulation ages fastest at the hottest point of the winding.

steps.inputs: Hot-spot temperature
steps.settings: F_AA = exp(15000/383 − 15000/(hot-spot + 273)). Equals 1 at 110 °C; above 1 means faster ageing.
steps.why: Says how many hours of normal life each real hour uses up.

steps.inputs: F_AA, daily capsules
steps.settings: Average F_AA × 24 h (or the time integral of F_AA) per day.
steps.why: Adds up the wear day by day.

steps.inputs: Daily equivalent hours, age at the start of the data
steps.settings: Sum the equivalent hours and divide by 8,760 to get years; add the age before the data began (extrapolated to installation year). Percent loss of life = equivalent hours ÷ normal insulation life × 100.
steps.output: True (thermal) age in years and % loss of life
steps.why: This is the number to compare with the 40-year design life.

steps.inputs: F_AA (or hot-spot temperature)
steps.settings: F_AA greater than 1, or hot-spot above 110 °C.
steps.why: Shows which loading events are eating the life.

steps.settings: Colour points by ambient temperature.
steps.why: Confirms the heat-run data behaves as expected before trusting the age.

steps.inputs: True age, average F_AA for every transformer
steps.settings: Colour by true age against calendar age; swap the worksheet across all transformers.
steps.why: Replace the transformers that are truly old, not just old on paper.

cases.title: Fixed bed catalyst end-of-run prediction
problem: In a fixed-bed reactor the catalyst slowly loses activity. To keep the reaction going, operators raise the temperature, until it reaches the reactor's maximum operating temperature and the catalyst must be regenerated or replaced. Planning that date well helps both short-term and long-term economics.

Doing it needs a normalised weighted average bed temperature (WABT), a choice of past data to train the correlation, and automatic updates with new data. Without Seeq, engineers combined data in spreadsheets and spent hours or days formatting and filtering it and removing times when equipment was out of service.
Data available: process data from OSIsoft PI, PHD and others; catalyst and reactor design data from the asset database or entered in Seeq as scalars or signals.
cases.solution: Remove shutdowns and non-steady periods, and mark each catalyst cycle between replacements or regenerations. Calculate WABT from first principles and normalise it for feed rate, feed and product quality, treat gas ratio and hydrogen partial pressure, so only catalyst ageing is left. Model normalised WABT against time in the current cycle with the Prediction tool, and read off the date it will reach the maximum operating temperature.
cases.sourceNote: Every step here is described on the page. The exact WABT and normalisation equations, settings and Formula expressions come from the notebook and the Seeq Knowledge Base; the page does not print them.

steps.inputs: Feed rate (or recycle gas compressor status)
steps.settings: Feed above a minimum; ignore short gaps; long maximum capsule.
steps.why: Startups and shutdowns would distort the trend and the model.

steps.inputs: Dates of catalyst changes or regenerations
steps.settings: One capsule from each fresh start to the end of that run, plus the current cycle.
steps.why: Each cycle ages from fresh catalyst, so cycles must not be mixed.

steps.inputs: Inlet and outlet temperature of each bed, catalyst amount per bed
steps.settings: Average each bed's inlet and outlet, then weight by the catalyst in that bed.
steps.why: Represents the temperature the catalyst as a whole works at.

steps.inputs: WABT, feed rate, feed and product quality, treat gas ratio, H2 partial pressure, reference values
steps.settings: Add correction terms that move WABT to standard conditions; the coefficients come from site kinetics.
steps.why: Without it, a feed or rate change looks like catalyst ageing.

steps.inputs: Current cycle capsule
steps.settings: Days since the start of the current cycle.
steps.why: The model needs time as its input.

steps.inputs: Target: normalised WABT. Input: days in cycle.
steps.settings: Linear (or polynomial) OLS; training window inside the current cycle; Limit to condition = Steady State; daily refresh.
steps.output: Predicted normalised WABT, carried into the future
steps.why: The slope is the deactivation rate; extending it shows where WABT is heading.

steps.inputs: Predicted normalised WABT and the maximum operating temperature
steps.settings: Predicted WABT is greater than or equal to the limit (for example 410 °C).
steps.output: A capsule whose start is the predicted end of run
steps.why: The page says the end-of-cycle prediction is the date predicted WABT goes above the maximum temperature.

steps.inputs: Normalised WABT for every cycle
steps.settings: Overlay cycles from their own start; record the steps in the Journal.
steps.output: A cycle-by-cycle comparison and documented method
steps.why: Shows if this run is ageing faster than earlier ones; the Journal lets others review and repeat it.

cases.title: Continuous manufacturing of pharmaceuticals
problem: For more than 50 years medicines have been made in batches. Many companies are now moving to continuous manufacturing, which the FDA encourages, because tighter control should give better quality, more efficiency, faster time to market and better patient protection.

In a continuous process it is hard to bring data together across many assets, including process analytical technology (PAT) instruments. KPIs must be watched in near real time to keep the process inside its approved design space and to adjust before anything drifts out. This company needed a dashboard to track the process and spot deviations as they happen.
Data available: process data in OSIsoft PI.
cases.solution: Quality engineers built a continuously updating dashboard. It removes data from equipment that is offline, shifts signals in time so each piece of material lines up with its own quality data, flags deviations from the design space and idle time, and calculates how long until an operator must do a manual task such as refilling a reagent tank. Results are shown on a colour-coded dashboard on the production floor and in a standard daily report.

cases.title: Continuous drug product Quality by Design (QbD) modeling
problem: Drug makers must keep critical process parameters, such as temperature or agitation, inside required ranges. If one is out of range, the batch fails, which can mean millions of dollars of rework and lost revenue.

Quality by Design (QbD) looks at several variables and how they interact. Using models from experiments, one variable may go wider if the others are in range: for example a 5-degree temperature deviation may be fine for quality if the rest are within limits. This expands the design space and cuts the number of major or critical deviations, each of which can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

When a product moves from R&D to a commercial plant, much of the design knowledge is lost through different equipment and people. A major drug maker wanted to improve its QbD modelling in R&D and carry that knowledge into production. Data available: lab results in Microsoft SQL, process data in OSIsoft PI.
cases.solution: Take the Design of Experiments (DOE) data from a continuous wet granulation step. Shift each signal in time according to where its sensor sits on the line, keep only steady-state operation, and build a model in Seeq's Prediction tool for the critical quality attributes (CQAs). Then apply that multivariate design space to commercial production as a boundary for continuous monitoring, flagging any deviation as a capsule.
cases.sourceNote: Every step is described on the page. Settings, model form and Formula expressions come from the notebook and the Seeq Knowledge Base. Figures such as '30 minutes per engineer per day' belong to other Seeq pages, not this one.

cases.title: Water treatment sand filter monitoring
problem: A city water utility takes river water, passes it fast through sand filters that trap solids, and sends it to a reservoir. About every four days each filter is cleaned by backwashing: clean water is pushed backwards through the sand and the dirt goes out with the wastewater.

The team tracked filters in an old, complex spreadsheet that was rarely updated, so run lengths between backwashes and backwash rates were changed only a couple of times a year. Wrong run lengths let solids sink deep into the sand, which eventually means an expensive shutdown to replace the media. The utility wanted more consistent filters, to spot poor performers and plan maintenance, and to use less clean water for backwashing, while also producing regulatory reports (including a larger report every four years).
Data available: Wonderware Historian (flows, valve positions, turbidity and more).
cases.solution: Clean the data, split each filter's operation into its four stages with conditions, and calculate metrics for each run, such as Unit Filter Run Volume (UFRV) and the cost of each backwash. Overlay backwash cycles over each other and compare filters, copy the analysis to every filter with an asset structure, and produce auto-updating daily and monthly reports that colour each run against site and state goals.
cases.sourceNote: Every step and tool is listed on the page. The names of the four stages, the UFRV and cost formulas, and the turbidity limit come from the notebook, the Seeq Knowledge Base and Wikipedia.

steps.inputs: Raw flow and turbidity

cases.title: Wind turbine curtailment and ramp-up losses
problem: Grid operators sometimes 'curtail' wind farms: the wind is there, but the power is not taken, because demand is low or the lines are congested. The wind company may charge the utility for revenue lost during curtailment.

But after a shutdown a wind turbine takes six to eight hours to ramp back up to full output, and that time also loses money. Spreadsheets could not pick out curtailment and ramp-up periods accurately, especially across a fleet. One wind company had curtailments about every two days, costing several hundred dollars a day, roughly $3,000 per month per wind farm, and could not quantify it.
Data available: OSIsoft PI and MySQL process data, organised with PI Asset Framework.
cases.solution: Work out how much power each turbine could have made from the wind speed and direction (its generation potential). Mark curtailment periods, then mark the ramp-up from the end of each curtailment until the turbine reaches its potential again. Compare potential with actual power in those windows, add up the lost energy for the chargeback, and run the same analysis across hundreds of turbines with PI Asset Framework.

cases.title: Well completion analysis (ISIP)
problem: Getting a well ready to produce takes a lot of engineering. Well spacing and the perforations along the pipe must be optimised, and wells interact with the reservoir and with each other.

A key number is the Instantaneous Shut-In Pressure (ISIP), the pressure right after pumping stops in each fracturing stage. Engineers used to print the pressure trend, draw a line by hand and read off the ISIP: about one hour per calculation and ten hours per well. Across hundreds or thousands of wells this was slow, error-prone and sometimes not done at all. A super major US oil and gas company wanted it faster.
Data available: OSIsoft PI pressure and pumping data, organised in OSIsoft Asset Framework.
cases.solution: Clean the pressure data, separate each well on a 'zipper' system (where several wells on one pad are fractured in turn), and mark each fracturing stage and the time just after shut-in as capsules. Calculate ISIP from the average pressure just after the stage, and Delta Pressure as ISIP minus the settled pressure. Compare ISIP curves across wells and repeat for every well with the asset framework.

steps.settings: Valve open AND pumping rate above a threshold.
steps.output: An Active Treatment condition per well
steps.why: On a zipper pad the pressure belongs to whichever well is being treated.

steps.inputs: Pumping (slurry) rate within the well's active time
steps.settings: Rate above a threshold (for example 10 bbl/min), ignore gaps shorter than 2 minutes, maximum 12 hours.
steps.why: Gives the exact start and end of every stage.

steps.settings: A short window starting at the end of each stage (for ISIP), and a later window (for settled pressure).
steps.why: ISIP must be read right after the pumps stop, before the pressure leaks off.

steps.settings: Average; timestamp at start; step interpolation.
steps.why: The page calculates ISIP from the average pressure after the stage.

steps.inputs: Clean pressure in the Settled windows; ISIP
steps.settings: Average settled pressure; Delta = ISIP − settled pressure.
steps.why: Gives engineers more insight into how the well is behaving.

steps.settings: Overlay stages from pump stop; swap the worksheet across all wells.

cases.title: Batch quality prediction (biopharma)
problem: A large molecule (biologic) drug maker checks each batch by sending samples to a lab. The lab result takes several hours, so engineers only learn whether a batch met its yield and quality targets after the batch has finished.
By then it is too late to change anything. A lost batch costs hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars, and running without feedback also wastes energy and raw materials.
Data available: process data (reactor temperature, volume, concentration) in PI, batch start and end times as PI Event Frames, and lab results in a Microsoft SQL database.
cases.solution: Predict the yield from process data before the lab result arrives. Seeq looks only at the reactor heating step of each batch, works out one average temperature, volume and concentration per batch, and fits a model of yield using only the parameters that are statistically significant. The model then runs online on every new batch, so an abnormal batch is flagged while operators can still adjust it.

cases.title: Real-time production potential (RTPP) for wind turbines
problem: A wind farm must tell the grid operator how much power it could produce right now. The usual estimate comes from the manufacturer's power curve (power for each wind speed).

Real turbines do not follow that curve exactly: parts age, the anemometer (wind speed sensor) on the turbine can read wrong, and turbulence changes the output. With an inaccurate estimate it is hard to plan production.
Data available: turbine power, wind speed, fault codes and status in OSIsoft PI.
cases.solution: Learn each turbine's real power curve from its own history with Seeq's Prediction tool. Train it only on clean periods: the turbine is communicating, producing power and not curtailed (held back) by the grid operator, and the site could produce more. The trained model gives Real-Time Production Potential (RTPP): what the turbine could produce now, even while it is curtailed.

The model learns the held-back output and under-predicts. Always limit training to the Training Data condition (step 4).
Treating curtailment stops as faults

Never re-checking the model
Parts age and sensors drift. Compare RTPP with actual power in normal operation (step 9) and retrain when the gap grows.
