cases.title: Bearing failure prediction
problem: Bearings in pumps, fans and compressors often fail fast: wear grows exponentially and gives little notice. The downtime is expensive and makes maintenance hard to plan.
Machines are linked, so when one bearing fails it often takes other bearings with it. Catching the first failure early prevents most of the damage.

Data available: vibration and process data in a historian such as OSIsoft PI, an asset structure such as PI AF to scale from one bearing to many, and high-frequency vendor test data uploaded to Seeq as CSV files.
cases.solution: Two teams share one workflow. Process experts in Seeq Workbench remove downtime from the vibration data, mark normal operation, set statistical limits from it and flag when any bearing goes past its limit. Data scientists then pull that clean, labelled data into Seeq Data Lab, train a neural network that outputs a 1-0 anomaly signal for each bearing, scale it to every bearing on site and push the signals back to Workbench for daily monitoring.
cases.sourceNote: The page lists the tools and the order of work but not the settings. Tag names, the 3-sigma limit, durations and the example numbers were worked out with the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base and the related Pump Health Monitoring and ID Fan pages.

steps.inputs: Motor power (or speed / run status)
steps.settings: Power below a 'stopped' level, for example 5 kW. Maximum capsule duration such as 1 day.
steps.why: A stopped machine shows near-zero vibration, which would drag the averages and limits down.

steps.inputs: Raw vibration and Downtime
steps.settings: Remove the downtime periods from the vibration signal.
steps.why: The page says vibration signals were cleansed to remove downtime before anything else.

steps.inputs: Cleansed vibration, load or speed, a known healthy period
steps.settings: Keep steady running at normal load inside a period with no known bearing problems.
steps.why: This is the reference for the limits and the training data for the neural network.

steps.inputs: Cleansed vibration over Normal Operation
steps.settings: Mean and standard deviation of vibration in normal operation; limit = mean + 3 × standard deviation.
steps.output: A Vibration Limit signal for each bearing
steps.why: A limit taken from each bearing's own normal behaviour fits it better than one fixed number for all.

steps.inputs: Cleansed vibration and its limit
steps.settings: Vibration above the limit; ignore events shorter than, for example, 1 hour.
steps.output: A Deviation condition for each bearing
steps.why: Flags when one bearing leaves normal behaviour; the minimum duration stops single spikes raising alarms.

steps.inputs: Deviation conditions of all bearings on the machine
steps.settings: Union (A or B or …).
steps.why: The page uses this to see when any bearing in the system deviates, since one failure leads to others.

steps.inputs: Cleansed vibration signals and the Normal Operation condition
steps.settings: Pull the data with the SPy library, train a neural network on normal operation, output 1 for anomaly and 0 for normal, push the result back to Workbench.
steps.output: A 1-0 Anomaly signal per bearing in Workbench
steps.why: The network can spot unusual patterns across several signals that one simple limit would miss.

steps.inputs: The single-bearing analysis
steps.settings: Repeat the calculations and the model for every bearing in the asset tree.
steps.output: Limits, deviations and anomaly signals for all bearings at the site
steps.why: Building it once and scaling it is far faster than building each bearing by hand.

steps.inputs: Anomaly signals, deviation conditions, vibration trends
steps.settings: Several dashboards for different levels of the organisation; set to update automatically.
steps.output: Daily monitoring view for the machinery engineer and summaries for managers
steps.why: The page says the engineer uses the anomaly signals in daily monitoring and the results sit in an Organizer Topic.

mistakes: Leaving downtime in the data
Zero vibration while stopped pulls the mean and limit down and causes false alarms at every start. Remove downtime first (steps 1 and 2).
Alarming on single spikes
A bump or a sensor glitch triggers an alarm. Use a minimum duration in the deviation search.
Building each bearing by hand
Hundreds of hand-typed limits cannot be maintained. Use the asset tree to scale one tested analysis (step 8).
cases.reported: Maintenance is told about abnormal operation several days before a catastrophic failure. The warning allows greasing to extend run life, ordering parts in advance and planning people, so cost and downtime are lower when the failure comes. For a critical refrigeration compressor, preventing a single bearing failure may save more than $0.5M in lost time.
cases.assumptions: The page does not give tag names, how normal operation is defined, the statistical limit used, the neural network design, or the dashboard layout. Mean + 3 sigma and the 1-hour minimum are common choices, not stated by Seeq.

cases.title: Batch tracking and cycle time analysis
problem: A batch of chemicals goes through several phases (for example charge, heat, react, cool, discharge). Cutting even a few minutes from a phase means more batches per year and more profit.

A large chemical maker tried to analyse phase times in Excel. Phases and idle times were hard to define, the wrong periods were often captured, the work could not be shared, and checking thousands of past batches by hand was impossible.
Data available: level, temperature and flow signals, and batch state text (string) signals from the control system, in the plant historian.
cases.solution: Let Seeq cut every batch in history into phases using process variables, Formula and string signals. Then measure each phase, compare it with past averages and the best batches, flag phases that run long, and turn idle time into lost money. A scorecard and an auto-updating dashboard replace the spreadsheet in operations meetings, and Seeq Journal records how it was built.
cases.sourceNote: The page lists the cleansing, calculations and reporting but not settings or phase names. Phase names, limits, the 20 % rule and the example were worked out with the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base and the related golden batch pages.

steps.inputs: Level, temperature and flow
steps.settings: Agile filter (or low-pass) with a window of a few minutes.
steps.why: The page filters noise first; noisy signals make phase searches flicker on and off and create tiny false phases.

steps.inputs: Batch state text signal from the control system
steps.settings: State equals each phase name, for example 'HEAT'. Maximum capsule duration such as 1 day.
steps.output: A condition for each phase that the control system names
steps.why: Where the control system already labels phases, this is the simplest and most reliable way to find them.

steps.inputs: Smoothed process variables
steps.settings: For phases with no label, use the physics: for example Charge = feed flow above 0.5 for at least 1 minute.
steps.output: Charge, Heat, React, Cool and Discharge conditions
steps.why: The page defines phases with process variables so the same rule works on every batch in history.

steps.inputs: Charge (start) and Discharge (end)
steps.settings: Join from the start of Charge to the end of the next Discharge.
steps.output: A Batch condition: one capsule per batch
steps.why: Gives the whole batch window, needed for idle time and total cycle time.

steps.inputs: Batch and all phase conditions
steps.settings: Inside a batch: Batch minus all phases. Between batches: time outside Batch.
steps.output: In-batch Idle and Between-batch Idle conditions
steps.why: Idle time is hidden in a spreadsheet; the page found it was the main thing to remove.

steps.inputs: Each phase and idle condition
steps.settings: Statistic: Duration, in minutes. Then the average and the minimum over a long history period for each phase.
steps.output: Phase Duration signals, plus Historical Average and Best for each phase
steps.why: These are the benchmarks the page compares each batch against.

steps.inputs: Phase duration and its historical average
steps.settings: Duration more than 20 % above the average.
steps.why: Flags abnormally long phases so engineers can find the cause and remove variability.

steps.inputs: Extra minutes over the benchmark, average cycle time, value per batch
steps.settings: Extra minutes as a share of a batch, times the value of a batch.
steps.output: A Lost Value signal ($ per batch)
steps.why: The page quantifies downtime as lost value, which tells managers where capital and effort pay most.

steps.inputs: Smoothed signals and phase conditions
steps.settings: Overlay all batches from batch start (or phase start).
steps.output: Every batch on one chart with its phases coloured
steps.why: The page stresses instant visual feedback: engineers can see at once whether each phase window is right for all batches.

steps.inputs: Phase and idle durations per batch
steps.settings: Condition scorecard over Batch, green at or below the average, red above the 20 % limit; dashboard set to update automatically; build steps written in Journal.
steps.output: A batch monitoring scorecard and live dashboard
steps.why: Used in operations meetings without updating spreadsheets, and future engineers can follow how it was built.

example.caption: One batch versus the historical average (batch value $30,000)
rows: Cool / Discharge / idle before next batch
200 min vs average 175 min: 25 min extra
Long phase flags (more than 20 % over average)
Discharge 20 vs 15 min (+33 %) and idle 15 vs 10 min (+50 %) are flagged; Heat 45 vs 40 (+12.5 %) is not
example.note: All numbers are made up for teaching.

mistakes: Searching on raw, noisy signals
Value Search then creates many tiny false phases. Smooth first (step 1).
Defining phases by hand-typed times
Fixed timestamps do not scale to thousands of batches. Use rules on process variables or state signals so every batch is cut the same way.
Ignoring idle time
Looking only at active phases misses the waiting inside and between batches, which is often the easiest time to win back (step 5).
cases.reported: Seeq helped the manufacturer remove idle time within batches and time between batches. Small cycle time gains and less batch-to-batch variation have a large financial effect over time. The page's example: 10 batches a day at 2.4 hours (144 minutes) each is 3,640 batches a year; cutting 10 minutes gives 10.7 batches a day or 3,912 a year, almost 300 more batches. At an average value of $20,000 to $50,000 per batch, this is substantial. The company has made many improvements of this type.
cases.assumptions: The page does not name the phases, signals, limits or batch value used. The page's own example arithmetic is slightly loose (10 × 365 = 3,650), but the point holds: a 10-minute cut adds roughly 270 to 300 batches a year.

cases.title: Faster R&D of pharma production lines
problem: To earn back the cost of a new drug, a company must bring it to market fast. Development needs many lab experiments and pilot batches, run in bioreactors (tanks where cells grow and make the drug).

Comparing old experiments meant merging data by hand in spreadsheets and spending hours or days lining up timestamps, with lots of room for error. It was quicker to run a new experiment than to compare the old ones.
Data available: process data from a DeltaV OPC-HDA historian (dissolved oxygen and other bioreactor signals) and cell counts from a Vi-CELL XR cell counter, saved as text files.
cases.solution: Connect both data sources in Seeq and give every experiment run its own capsule. Smooth the noisy dissolved oxygen signal, use an integral to get total oxygen uptake per run, and divide oxygen uptake by the number of cells to get the cell-specific oxygen uptake rate. This number can be compared fairly between small lab bioreactors and the larger pilot bioreactor. A golden batch of cell growth rate becomes the yardstick for future experiments and scale-up.
cases.sourceNote: The page names the calculations (capsule per run, smoothing, DO integral, cell-specific oxygen uptake rate, golden batch, overlay) but not the settings. The run search, smoothing window, units and example values were worked out with the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base and the related batch quality pages.

steps.inputs: DeltaV OPC-HDA historian; Vi-CELL XR text files
steps.settings: Connect the historian; import the cell counter files with the sample time and viable cell density columns, using the same time zone.
steps.output: Dissolved oxygen and other bioreactor signals, plus a Viable Cell Density signal
steps.why: Removes the hours of copying and timestamp alignment in spreadsheets.

steps.inputs: Agitator speed (or the run status tag) for each bioreactor
steps.settings: Speed above, for example, 50 rpm; maximum capsule duration about 14 days; name capsules by vessel and run.
steps.output: A Runs condition: one capsule per experiment or pilot batch
steps.why: The page creates a capsule for each batch or experiment; every later number is calculated per run.

steps.inputs: Dissolved oxygen (DO)
steps.settings: Agile filter with a window of tens of minutes; check the smoothed line still follows real changes.
steps.why: DO probes are noisy; rates calculated from raw DO jump around.

steps.inputs: Oxygen uptake rate (OUR) and Runs
steps.settings: Integral of OUR inside each run, restarting at the start of each run.
steps.output: A Total Oxygen Uptake signal per run
steps.why: The page uses an integral to get a total oxygen uptake trend, which is also smoother than the raw signal.

steps.inputs: Viable cell density samples
steps.settings: Join the few daily cell counts into a continuous line (linear or step interpolation) so it can be divided at any time.
steps.output: A continuous Viable Cell Density signal
steps.why: Cell counts come only a few times a day; without this, division gives values only at sampling times.

steps.inputs: OUR and Viable Cell Density
steps.settings: Divide oxygen uptake by cell density; convert to pmol per cell per hour.
steps.output: A Cell-Specific Oxygen Uptake Rate signal
steps.why: Dividing by the number of cells removes the effect of vessel size and cell count, so 2 L and 100 L runs can be compared.

steps.inputs: Viable Cell Density
steps.settings: Growth rate = change in the natural log of cell density per hour.
steps.why: Growth rate is what the golden batch is built from on the page.

steps.inputs: Cell Growth Rate over the best runs
steps.settings: Training: chosen good runs; statistics: average with upper and lower bands (for example ±3 standard deviations).
steps.output: A golden batch profile with limits
steps.why: Lets the team see at once whether a new experiment or scale-up batch grows like the best runs.

steps.inputs: Cell-Specific Oxygen Uptake Rate for runs at different scales
steps.settings: Line up all runs from their start; colour by vessel size.
steps.output: An overlay of lab and pilot runs
steps.why: On the page this overlay made the different growth curve of the 100 L bioreactor clearly visible.

steps.inputs: Overlays, golden batch, per-run results
steps.settings: Write the findings next to the analysis and share the document.
steps.output: A shared record of experiments and scale-up findings
steps.why: Helps the team refine results, design better experiments and compare runs during scale-up.

rows: 2 L lab run: OUR 5.0 mmol/L/h, cells 10 million per mL
0.005 ÷ 10,000,000,000 cells/L = 0.50 pmol per cell per hour
100 L pilot run: OUR 3.6 mmol/L/h, cells 9 million per mL
0.0036 ÷ 9,000,000,000 cells/L = 0.40 pmol per cell per hour

mistakes: Dividing by raw cell count samples
Without interpolation the result exists only at sample times. Make the cell count continuous first (step 5).
Integrating across all time
Total oxygen uptake then keeps adding up across many runs. Restart the integral at the start of each run (step 4).
Over-smoothing DO
A very wide smoothing window hides real changes during fast growth. Compare raw and smoothed lines before using them.

The overlay of cell-specific oxygen uptake rates for different bioreactor scales clearly showed the different growth curve of the 100 L bioreactor.

cases.title: Detect drilling oscillations
problem: Oil and gas companies hire contract drillers, who use an auto-driller: a control system that sets drilling depth and speed with little human input. Drillers often leave it on default settings and hold one speed for long periods.

With the wrong settings the auto-driller itself causes vibration (oscillation). Sustained vibration damages the rig and the well, causing costly repairs and delays. The company could only react after damage, and could not easily tell drillers which set points, gain and decay settings to use.
Data available: drilling data in OSIsoft PI, organised by rig and well in OSIsoft Asset Framework.
cases.solution: Find oscillations in the drilling block speed and count them. Seeq smooths the block speed, takes its rate of change to spot each quick speed ramp-up, merges ramp-ups that follow each other into one oscillation episode, and totals oscillation time and on-bottom drilling time per shift and per day. A Seeq Topic shows where and when problems happened (by well, depth, equipment and time of day), so engineers can guide the drillers every day.
cases.sourceNote: The page lists the steps (agile filter, derivative, Value Search, merging capsules, Scorecard Metric for on-bottom time, Topic per shift and day) but not settings. Thresholds, the merge gap, shift times and the on-bottom rule were worked out with the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base.

steps.inputs: Block speed, on-bottom status or weight on bit, bit depth, for each rig and well
steps.settings: Browse the asset tree so the same calculations attach to every well.
steps.output: Signals organised by rig and well
steps.why: Lets one analysis run across all wells and be split by well and equipment later.

steps.inputs: Drilling block speed
steps.settings: Agile filter with a short window (for example 1 minute).
steps.why: The page smooths first; the rate of change of a noisy signal is mostly noise.

steps.inputs: Smoothed block speed
steps.settings: First derivative (rate of change).
steps.why: The page uses the derivative to show 'ramp-up' times, when the auto-driller suddenly speeds up.

steps.inputs: Speed Rate
steps.settings: Rate above a ramp-up limit; maximum capsule duration such as 10 minutes.
steps.output: A Ramp-Ups condition: one capsule per single oscillation
steps.why: Each capsule is one ramp-up, so they can be counted.

steps.inputs: Ramp-Ups
steps.settings: Merge capsules that are less than, for example, 2 minutes apart.
steps.why: The page merges adjacent capsules so a run of back-to-back ramp-ups counts as one sustained oscillation with a true duration.

steps.inputs: Weight on bit (or on-bottom status)
steps.settings: Weight on bit above a small limit, meaning the bit is on the bottom of the hole and drilling.
steps.why: Oscillation only matters while actually drilling; time spent on connections or trips should not count.

steps.inputs: Rig time zone
steps.settings: 12-hour shifts (for example 07:00 and 19:00) and daily periods.
steps.why: The page reports totals per shift and per day.

steps.inputs: On-Bottom, Oscillation Episodes, Ramp-Ups, bounded by Shift
steps.settings: Condition metrics: total duration of On-Bottom, total duration of Oscillation Episodes, count of Ramp-Ups.
steps.output: A table per shift: on-bottom hours, oscillation minutes, number of oscillations
steps.why: The page aggregates the on-bottom condition with Scorecard Metric and summarises time and number of oscillations by shift.

steps.inputs: Oscillation minutes and on-bottom minutes per shift
steps.settings: Oscillation minutes divided by on-bottom minutes, times 100.
steps.why: One easy number to compare shifts, rigs and wells.

steps.inputs: Shift and daily tables, oscillation time by depth band, well and equipment
steps.settings: Daily report; histograms of oscillation time by depth and by time of day.
steps.output: A near real-time report for engineers and the operator overseeing drilling
steps.why: Shows the highest-risk wells and depths, so engineers can recommend set points, gain and decay settings to the drillers.

rows: 8.0 h = 480 min (the other 4 h were connections and trips)

mistakes: Taking the derivative of the raw signal
Noise becomes hundreds of false ramp-ups. Smooth first (step 2).
Not merging ramp-ups
Many tiny capsules hide how long the rig really oscillated. Merge nearby ramp-ups into episodes (step 5).
Dividing by the whole shift
Connection and trip time dilutes the result. Divide by on-bottom time.
cases.reported: Seeq lets the company reduce auto-driller vibration problems through visualisation and notifications. Making proactive changes backed by data extends the life of the equipment. Fewer oscillation events significantly reduce drilling costs. The results are longer bit run times, fewer delays due to trips, more efficient drilling and lower costs. The company can now adjust drilling in near real time instead of reacting after damage, and drill holes much faster without causing damage, saving time and money.

cases.title: Monitor batch quality from a reference profile (brewery)
problem: Beer tastes right only if its diacetyl (a buttery-tasting chemical made by yeast) is at the right level. For lagers, brewers do a 'diacetyl rest': they raise the temperature at the end of fermentation so the yeast removes it.

Diacetyl is tested in a lab, far less often than temperature is measured, and results come late. So the temperature during the rest is the best live sign of quality. A large brewery wanted to compare each batch's temperature with that of past good batches and correct a batch that drifts.
Data available: fermentation and diacetyl rest operations as OSIsoft PI Event Frames, temperature in OSIsoft PI, and diacetyl lab results in SQL.
cases.solution: Pick five past batches with good quality and build a reference profile from them: the average temperature curve with limits at plus and minus three standard deviations. Apply the profile to every new batch with live temperature data. A deviation search marks every time a batch leaves the band, and a scorecard and trend show the limits, so engineers can adjust while the batch is still running.
cases.sourceNote: The page names the five good batches, the average and ±3 standard deviation profiles, the deviation search and the scorecard. Gridding, durations and the example numbers were worked out with the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base.

steps.inputs: Fermentation and Diacetyl Rest event frames
steps.settings: Add both as conditions; keep the batch ID as a capsule property.
steps.why: The profile is built and applied over the diacetyl rest of each batch.

steps.inputs: Diacetyl lab results per batch; Diacetyl Rest condition
steps.settings: Look at the lab results and pick five batches with good diacetyl; make a condition holding only their rest periods.
steps.why: The page uses five historical good batches as the reference; including a poor batch would widen the band.

steps.inputs: Temperature; training condition Good Batches
steps.settings: Statistic: Average; gridding period such as 5 minutes; apply to the Diacetyl Rest condition.
steps.output: An Average Temperature profile that repeats for every batch
steps.why: The expected temperature at each hour of the rest, lined up from the start of the rest.

steps.inputs: Same as step 3
steps.settings: Statistic: standard deviation, multiplier +3 and −3.
steps.why: The page uses ±3 standard deviations as the boundary of statistically good batches.

steps.inputs: Live temperature and the upper and lower limits
steps.settings: Temperature above the upper limit; a second search for below the lower limit.
steps.output: Too Hot and Too Cold conditions
steps.why: The page's deviation search creates capsules for boundary excursions.

steps.inputs: Too Hot and Too Cold
steps.settings: Union (A or B).
steps.why: One condition to count and alert on, whichever side the batch leaves.

cases.title: Haul truck analysis at a tank battery
problem: When natural gas is produced, liquid hydrocarbons are separated out and stored in tanks at a 'tank battery'. How fast the tanks fill depends on how much the wells produce.

Where there is no pipeline, the liquid must be taken away by truck. Each truck haul costs money under a logistics contract, but too few hauls risks overfilling a tank. Hauls were tracked by hand, and trucks were sometimes booked twice for the same tank.
Data available: tank levels and other process data in OSIsoft PI.
cases.solution: Use the tank level to see every truck load and to plan the next one. Seeq smooths the level so its rate of change is reliable, spots each truck loading from the sudden drop in level, calculates how much each truck took, compares the number of hauls with the liquid produced, and watches how fast the tank is filling so hauls can be booked in the logistics system at the right time.

cases.title: Salt deposition risk monitoring
problem: In refinery crude and FCC fractionator overheads and hydroprocessing effluent trains, ammonium salts (NH4Cl and NH4HS) can come out of the gas as solids when the stream gets too cold. They cause corrosion and foul or plug trays, exchangers and pipes, which can lead to loss of containment, safety risks and lost money.

Engineers need to know when the unit runs in a high-risk condition, shown as a continuous signal of 'percent of time at risk'. Before Seeq this meant combining lab and process data from separate systems in a spreadsheet, taking hours or days.
Data available: process temperatures in a historian (OSIsoft PI, PHD or others) and lab results for H2S, NH3 and HCl in a SQL database.
cases.solution: Bring lab and process data together in Seeq, remove shutdowns and start-ups, and use Formula to calculate the salt deposition temperature (SDT) of each salt from the lab results. Compare the stream temperature with the SDT plus a safety margin; Deviation Search marks every at-risk period, and the result is trended as percent of time at risk and shown as a histogram.
cases.sourceNote: The page names the inputs, the SDT calculation, the first-principles limits, Deviation Search and the histogram, but not the equations or margins. The SDT formula below is a simplified teaching version with made-up constants; real units use a proper first-principles model.

Such outages can cause safety issues and millions of dollars of lost production opportunities. The tools can also help predict future failure events, allowing better planning and lower repair cost. Engineers spend less time collecting and analysing data and more time on improvements that reduce at-risk time.

cases.title: Lockout pressure optimization (pipeline)
problem: If an oil pipeline ruptures, the pressure on the discharge side of the pumping station drops. So operators set a low-pressure 'lockout': below this pressure the pipeline shuts down hard. A lockout can last hours or days and costs a lot of revenue.

Pressure also drops for normal reasons (process variation), which causes unnecessary lockouts. Working out the right lockout pressure for each station needs lots of cleaned data, which a spreadsheet cannot handle, so a major operator used an arbitrary 400 psi.
Data available: six months of station data in OSIsoft PI and CSV files.
cases.solution: Let the station's own data set the limit. Seeq marks when the station is running, removes bad data and start-up and shutdown transients, keeps only steady normal running, and finds the lowest pressure (the 1st percentile) in each running period. Percentile logic on these values gives a new, lower lockout pressure that still catches a real rupture. A Topic tracks it every quarter.
cases.sourceNote: The page gives the method (running capsules tuned to remove transients, 1st percentile per period, a table, percentile logic) and the result (400 to 308 psi), but not settings. Thresholds, trim times and the example were worked out with the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base.

steps.output: A table of lowest normal pressure by period
steps.why: The page reports the lowest pressure of each period in a table.

cases.title: Chromatography and transition analysis
problem: Chromatography is a key purification step in making protein drugs: the product comes out of a packed column as a 'peak' that is collected. A biotech company compared the quality and yield of each batch's peaks in Excel, which took a very long time.
Columns also wear out. If the packing degrades, separation gets worse and a whole batch can be lost, so column integrity and efficiency must be watched to predict failure.
Data available: Emerson DeltaV, OSIsoft PI and CSV files (UV absorbance, flow rate, conductivity).
cases.solution: Find every peak and every buffer change (transition) automatically with Profile Search. Calculate the mass in each peak from UV absorbance and flow and overlay peaks to compare batches. For column health, smooth and normalise the conductivity during each transition and calculate textbook column measures (HETP, Asymmetry, TransWidth, DirectAf). Auto-updating dashboards show yield, quality and column integrity in near real time.
cases.sourceNote: The page names the tools and methods but not the equations or limits. The formulas below are simplified textbook versions (assuming a Gaussian-shaped transition) for teaching; the company followed published literature methods.

steps.settings: Bring UV absorbance, flow and conductivity for each column into one worksheet.
steps.output: All column signals side by side
steps.why: Removes the manual copying into Excel.

steps.settings: Select one good peak as the pattern; similarity around 85 %.

steps.why: The page uses Profile Search to find chromatography peaks in every run.

steps.settings: Select one clean buffer step as the pattern.
steps.why: The page also finds transitions with Profile Search; these are used to test the column.

steps.settings: Concentration from UV times flow gives mass flow.
steps.why: The page calculates mass yield from UV absorbance and flow rate.

steps.output: A Peak Mass signal: grams per peak
steps.why: One yield number per batch to compare.

steps.settings: Agile filter with a short window that keeps the step edge sharp.
steps.why: The page applies an agile filter to conductivity before transition analysis.

steps.settings: Scale from 0 (old buffer) to 1 (new buffer).
steps.why: The page normalises traces for TransWidth and DirectAf so runs with different buffers can be compared.

steps.settings: Find the times at 10 %, 50 % and 90 %; then Asymmetry, plate count and HETP (and TransWidth, DirectAf) from published formulas.
steps.why: Rising HETP or asymmetry far from 1 means the packing is degrading.

UV absorbance is not mass. Apply the calibration factor and use the actual flow, which may change during elution.
Comparing transitions with different buffers
Raw conductivity levels differ between buffers. Normalise to 0 to 1 first (step 7).

cases.title: Valve health diagnostics (fleet)
problem: Valves are among the most common equipment in process plants, from small control valves in chemical plants to large pipeline and subsea valves. It is hard to judge in near real time how healthy each valve is.
Servicing valves on a calendar wastes effort and money, but skipping maintenance leads to failures, unplanned downtime, lost revenue and more safety and environmental risk.
Data available: valve position, controller mode and process data in OSIsoft PI; maintenance records in SAP.
cases.solution: Monitor every valve's condition from its own data. Seeq removes manual-mode and downtime data, smooths noisy signals, counts how often each valve reverses direction and how far it travels, and tracks metrics like stroke time and static friction (stiction). Combining the warning signs gives a health score per valve, so bad actors stand out on a Treemap and maintenance goes where it is needed.

cases.title: Multi-phase flow meter (MPFM) analysis
problem: A multi-phase flow meter (MPFM) measures oil, water and gas flowing together from a well, without separating them first. These meters are used to watch each well and to split production between owners when a field has several owners.
So their accuracy matters: a wrong meter means wrong well surveillance and wrong money split between owners. Problems must be found and fixed quickly.
Data available: meter flows, pressures and temperatures from Ignition SCADA.
cases.solution: Check the meters against each other continuously. Seeq corrects each meter's flow for expansion due to pressure and temperature, adds up all the MPFMs, and compares the total with the main separator flow (and sales measurements). Value Search marks every period with a large difference, and engineers look inside those periods for the cause.
cases.sourceNote: The page lists the steps (pressure and temperature correction, summing MPFMs, reconciling with the separator and sales, Value Search for large discrepancies) but not formulas or limits. cases.title: Filter membrane predictive maintenance
problem: Ultrafiltration membranes are fine filters that let liquid through and hold back the product (or the other way round). They are reused for many batches, with Clean-In-Place (CIP) washing between batches.
If cleaning does not work well, or the membrane slowly fouls or wears, batches take longer, product is lost because it cannot pass the filter, or quality suffers if the membrane fails.
Data available: pressures and flows in the OSIsoft PI platform; UV data in a SQL database.
cases.solution: Measure the membrane's health in every batch and predict when it will need maintenance. Seeq uses UV data and flow rates to tell batch operation from cleaning, applies Darcy's Law to calculate the membrane's resistance from pressures and flows during batches, and trends it. A prediction model extends the trend into the future with warning and alert limits, so maintenance can be planned before the membrane fails.
cases.sourceNote: The page names the mode separation, Darcy's Law resistance, the prediction model and the Organizer Topic. Thresholds, membrane area and the example numbers were worked out with the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base and related pages.

cases.title: Mass balance on process units
problem: A plant has many units, each with streams going in and out. A mass balance checks that what goes in equals what comes out (plus anything stored). It reveals leaks, faulty sensors, meters that need calibration and inefficient operation.
Many sites do not have this view. Those that do often use a method that is hard to maintain and does not update when new data arrives, so it cannot be used for continuous monitoring.
Data available: flow rates and other process data in the plant historian; stream properties such as density.
cases.solution: Let Seeq calculate the balance continuously. Convert every inlet and outlet flow to the same mass units, total them over a fixed period (for example each day), subtract total out from total in, and flag any period where the difference is larger than an agreed amount or percentage. A scorecard shows the balance as a table and an Organizer Topic keeps it on a dashboard.

cases.title: Induced-draft fan maintenance (cement)
problem: In a cement plant, induced-draft (ID) fans pull gas through the kiln, creating the draft that speeds up drying of the clinker. Over time dust scale builds up on the fan blades, which raises vibration until the fan can break down.

A large US building materials supplier had about one full day of unplanned ID fan downtime per quarter, at about $20,000 per hour, nearly $500,000 in total. Routine scheduled cleaning can also be unnecessary and expensive, and spreadsheets were too slow to predict failures.
Data available: fan vibration and process data in Wonderware Historian and OSIsoft PI.

The model updates as new data arrives, and overlaying the current cycle on past cycles helps troubleshoot vibration events.

problem: Critical process parameters (CPPs) are the settings and measurements that decide product quality, for example a reactor temperature. Manufacturers need statistical control limits for each CPP and must watch quality against fixed or changing specification limits.

Data available: process data in OSIsoft PI or another historian; quality and batch event data in a SQL database.

cases.title: Aggregate and analyze alarms
problem: Plants have many alarms. Engineers need to know how often each alarm fires and how alarms relate to each other, so they can fix the noisy ones and make sure real ones get attention, reducing upsets and unplanned downtime.
Alarm data usually sits in separate alarm databases, away from the process data needed to understand why alarms happen.
Data available: an alarm and event database (MS SQL Server) and a process historian (OSI PI, AspenTech IP21, Honeywell PHD and others).
cases.solution: Bring alarms and process data together in Seeq. Formula removes 'chattering' alarms (very short alarms that fire again and again close together) so only true alarms are counted. Alarms are grouped by type and period, and Scorecard Metrics give the alarm count and percent of time in alarm for each tag, combined in one colour-coded scorecard. cases.title: Aligning data for calculations and correlation
problem: In a plant, material takes time to travel: along conveyor belts, screw conveyors, pipes, plug flow reactors, extruders and analyzer sample lines. This delay is called dead time or transport delay. Lab (LIMS) results also arrive at irregular times after the process ran.

If data is not lined up, strong links between an upstream signal and a downstream result are hidden, models come out poor, and 'before and after' comparisons around an event (an additive switched on, a setpoint change) are wrong. Doing the alignment without good tools is slow and tedious.
Data available: process data in AspenTech IP21, Honeywell PHD or AVEVA PI System; quality data in LIMS.
cases.solution: Put every signal on a common time basis before calculating. Clean the data first, use Value Search to mark the starting events, measure or calculate the delay, and shift signals earlier or later with the move() Formula function, either by a fixed delay or by a delay stored as another signal. For lab results, join the process condition and the lab condition with Composite Condition, or with Formula using a matching ID when results come out of order.

problem: A large US building materials company had unexplained cement kiln stoppages. Unplanned stoppages usually happen about once a quarter, but once there were two multi-hour stoppages in five days. Each hour of stoppage costs about $20,000 in lost production.

A kiln can stop for many reasons: an induced-draft fan bearing failure, high pressure from a blockage, or chemical incompatibility. Engineers tried to find the causes with Excel charts and reports, which was cumbersome and did not get to the bottom of it.
Data available: process data in a Wonderware historian.
cases.solution: Let Seeq find every stoppage and line them up for comparison. The kiln feed flow is smoothed with the agile filter, and Value Search marks each stoppage as a capsule when feed flow is low. Engineers zoom into the time just before each stoppage and compare stoppages side by side to see whether the same cause keeps coming back. An Organizer Topic updates automatically and tells operators about new stoppages.

cases.title: Dynamic modeling and what-if analyses
problem: When you change something in a plant, the result does not appear at once. Tanks, pipes, conveyors and equipment design add a dead time (nothing happens for a while) and a lag (the change then builds up slowly).

Control engineers usually own this 'dynamic' modelling for loop tuning and advanced process control. Ordinary regression ignores the delays and lags, so it fits poorly, and dynamic modelling usually sits in specialised, hard-to-use software away from everyday data analysis.
Data available: process signals in the plant historian (feeds, ratios, inventories, analyser or lab composition).
cases.solution: Use Seeq Formula's time-delay and time-lag functions to build simple dynamic models such as first order plus dead time (FOPDT), and more complex ones, for both monitoring and prediction. The model can calculate product composition in real time for operators, and can be run with 'what-if' inputs to test better feed ratio or reactor inventory changes before trying them in the plant.
cases.sourceNote: The page names FOPDT, time-delay and time-lag functions in Formula, what-if analyses and a real-time composition display, but not functions or settings. The model numbers and formulas were worked out with the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base and standard process control.

Step +2 units at t = 2 and 5 min

Step +2 units at t = 35 min (three time constants)

The output answers minutes later, so a plain regression underestimates the effect. Add dead time and lag first.
Mixing up delay and lag

Fitting through shutdowns
Start-ups and trips are not the normal dynamics. Train only on clean steps in normal running.

cases.title: Emissions reporting during detector exceedance events
problem: Plants that emit certain pollutants must report them to environmental regulators under strict rules. When the measuring instrument goes down or goes 'out of range' (stuck at its maximum reading), the real pollutant level must be estimated and reported within a tight deadline.
These calculations were complex and done by hand, so an engineer had to drop everything (often at night) to do them.
Data available: detector and process data in a historian such as OSIsoft PI, Honeywell PHD or AspenTech IP21.
cases.solution: Let Seeq detect each exceedance event and do the estimate automatically. It removes readings outside the detector's range, finds when the detector is pegged at its limit, uses the rate of change just before and after to model the hidden part of the signal, and calculates the maximum concentration and the total mass released above the detector limit. An auto-updating Organizer Topic shares each event's results as a link or PDF.
cases.sourceNote: The page lists the steps (cleansing, Value Search for events, derivative, Formula model of the out-of-range signal, Signal from Condition and Scorecard for maximum and mass). The triangle model, the limit and the example were worked out with the notebook; a site's approved estimation method must be used for real reporting.

steps.settings: Treat the hidden part as a triangle: height above the limit = rise × fall × duration ÷ (rise + fall).

The flat 500 ppm line hides the real peak and under-reports emissions. Model the gap first.

Mixing per-hour flow with per-minute or per-second data gives answers off by 60 or 3,600 times. Check units carefully.

cases.title: Free lime soft sensor (cement)
problem: Free lime (unreacted lime left in the clinker) is a key quality number in cement making; most plants aim for 1 % to 2 %. The page says a high reading means raw materials and energy are wasted, while a low reading points to quality problems that can cost revenue and reputation.

Free lime is measured by sending a clinker sample to the lab, and the result takes at least an hour to reach the historian. That delay makes it hard for operators to tune the process, and alternative fuels such as shredded tyres and municipal waste make free lime even harder to control.
Data available: process data in Wonderware and OSIsoft PI; lab results in a laboratory data management system.
cases.solution: Build a 'soft sensor': a model that estimates free lime every minute from the NOx signal, which is measured continuously. Seeq smooths both signals with the agile filter, marks the training period with a condition, and uses the Prediction tool with NOx as input. The model updates automatically, so the operator sees near real-time free lime and can adjust fuel to cut waste while keeping clinker quality good.

cases.title: Control loop performance monitoring (CLPM)
problem: A plant has hundreds or thousands of automatic controllers (control loops) that should run without operators touching them. Most sites cannot see how these controllers actually perform: are they in automatic or has an operator put them in manual? Are they stable? Do they hold their setpoint?

Poor control increases safety and environmental risk, misses product specifications, lowers throughput, wastes energy and raw materials, raises maintenance costs and needs more operator intervention. Off-the-shelf CLPM tools cannot calculate metrics per recipe, grade or operating condition, cannot add other process tags, and offer limited metrics.
Data available: controller mode, output, setpoint and process variable in the process historian, plus recipe or grade tags.
cases.solution: Calculate controller performance metrics in Seeq from each loop's mode, output, setpoint and process variable: for example controller error, output travel, percent time in the correct mode and setpoint changes. Conditions for each recipe, grade or operating condition let each loop be judged against its own limits, and other process tags can be added. Scorecards, a Treemap and an Organizer Topic show which controllers need attention.
cases.sourceNote: The page names the metrics and the tools (Periodic Condition, Signal from Condition, Formula for benchmark limits, Value Search, Scorecard, Treemap, Organizer). Limits, the error formula and the example were worked out with the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base and the related valve health page.

cases.title: Loss monitoring and categorization
problem: Every plant loses performance: lost production, quality, energy, raw materials, and environmental or regulatory losses. These cut profit and can threaten the licence to operate.

Losses should be found, investigated, sorted by cause and summed up for benchmarking, planning and justifying projects. Done by hand, this can take an engineer up to a week a month for a single unit. One manufacturer wanted to see when equipment ran below capacity, why, and how much each cause cost.
Data available: production data in Honeywell PHD, OSIsoft PI or another historian; operator shift logs or a shutdown tracking database.
cases.solution: Let Seeq find and measure each loss automatically. Value Search marks every period when production is below target (periods at or above target are ignored). Losses that cross a month end are split between months. Signal from Condition calculates how much production each event lost, each event is placed in a reason-code bucket (by an operator or by rules), unassigned events are flagged, and histograms and scorecards sum the losses by category in a monthly Organizer report.

cases.title: Clinker production monitoring (cement)
problem: Clinker is the main ingredient of cement. A large US building materials supplier needed better production reports, especially to compare the calculated clinker yield with the measured total.
Building the reports in spreadsheets was slow and error-prone: staff had to filter out poor-quality clinker and outage periods by hand, and different clinker types need different calculations.
Data available: kiln feed, kiln slag and production signals in a Wonderware historian.
cases.solution: Let Seeq calculate clinker from the kiln feed and kiln slag signals, mark the shifts and operating modes when clinker was really produced, and total the tons per 12-hour shift, leaving out weekends and planned kiln outages. The report refreshes with the latest data each day and is shared across the company.

problem: To raise efficiency, engineers need to see how a batch process spends its time in each phase. Unproductive time, such as cleaning, maintenance and manual re-cleaning that differs from shift to shift, must be visible so it can be reduced; less waiting means more production and profit.

cases.title: Predict conveyor belt tensioning date (mining)
problem: Mines move ore on conveyor belts from the mine, through processing, to the ship. If a belt stops, deliveries are late and profit suffers.

Over time belt tension drops, the belt starts to wander from side to side, and soon after it fails. With 100 belts there is typically at least one failure a day. Re-tensioning every week wastes effort, but tension behaviour was hard to predict with older tools. A global mining company wanted to predict when each belt needs re-tensioning.
Data available: belt tension signals (left and right side) in OSIsoft PI, organised in OSIsoft Asset Framework.
cases.solution: Predict each belt's failure date from its tension. Seeq removes downtime and smooths the signals, averages left and right tension into a baseline, uses the derivative to spot the start of the end-of-life tension drop, trains a projection model on that drop and extends it forward, and finds when tension will fall below the low-tension limit (50 % of baseline, or as the expert sets) with a safety factor. Signal from Condition gives the time left, and a Treemap colours every belt red, yellow or green.

cases.title: Power plant boiler efficiency (fouling)
problem: In a power plant boiler, ash and scale slowly build up on the tubes. This is called fouling. It acts like a blanket, so the boiler needs more fuel to make the same steam. Knowing how fast fouling grows helps run the boiler better and plan cleaning.

Fouling is very hard to measure because the boiler never runs the same way for long: load, fuel and air change all the time. Engineers spent one year trying to build a fouling model in Excel and failed, then turned to Seeq.
Data available: steam output, fuel flow and other boiler signals from the plant historian. The page does not name the tags.
cases.solution: Compare like with like. Seeq sorts the operating data and keeps only the periods where all conditions are comparable (the page calls them "apples-to-apples" periods). In those periods it plots how hard the boiler works (fuel in) to make a given output (steam out). If the boiler needs more fuel for the same steam, it is fouling. The extra fuel is turned into dollars, the trend is projected forward to see when fouling becomes unacceptable, and the steps are saved in a Journal so the same analysis can be reused on other boilers.
cases.sourceNote: The page gives the idea (comparable periods, effort for a given output, dollar impact, prediction, Journal) but not the tools, tags or limits. The steps below were worked out by the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base pages. Treat them as one sensible way to build it.

steps.inputs: Steam flow and fuel flow
steps.settings: A moving-average or low-pass filter over about 15 minutes.
steps.why: Raw flows jump around. Without smoothing, later searches break into hundreds of tiny capsules.

steps.inputs: Smoothed steam flow
steps.settings: Steam between 90 and 110 t/h (the band around one chosen load). Ignore capsules shorter than about 1 hour.
steps.why: Fuel per tonne of steam changes with load, so only compare periods at the same load.

steps.n: Remove periods that are not normal
steps.inputs: Signals that show unusual running, such as sootblower on, burners out of service, or a trip
steps.settings: One search per unusual state; then combine them into one Not Normal condition.
steps.why: Startups, trips and soot blowing change fuel use for reasons other than fouling.

steps.inputs: Load Band and Not Normal
steps.settings: A outside B (Load Band minus Not Normal).
steps.why: This is the core idea of the page: every later number is worked out only when the boiler is running the same way.

steps.n: Calculate how hard the boiler works
steps.inputs: Smoothed fuel flow and smoothed steam flow
steps.settings: Fuel divided by steam.
steps.output: A Specific Fuel signal (tonnes of fuel per tonne of steam)
steps.why: One number that rises as fouling grows, whatever the load.

steps.inputs: Specific Fuel, bounded by Apples-to-Apples
steps.settings: Statistic: Average. Timestamp at the start. Interpolation: Step, not Linear.
steps.output: A Specific Fuel per Period signal
steps.why: Turns a noisy signal into one clean point per comparable period, so the slow fouling trend is easy to see.

steps.n: See the trend and the operating modes
steps.inputs: Specific Fuel per Period; fuel against steam inside Apples-to-Apples
steps.settings: Colour the points by operating mode or by month, and mark cleaning and treatment dates.
steps.output: A chart of boiler effort over time
steps.why: Shows which operating modes make fouling grow faster and how much each cleaning or treatment helps, two things the page says engineers learned.

steps.n: Turn the extra fuel into dollars
steps.inputs: Specific Fuel, a clean baseline value, steam flow and fuel price
steps.settings: (Specific Fuel minus clean baseline) times steam flow gives extra fuel per hour; times price gives dollars per hour; then a daily total.
steps.output: An Extra Fuel Cost signal and a daily cost
steps.why: Managers act on money, not on fuel ratios. The page says fouling impact was shown in dollars based on fuel cost.

steps.inputs: Specific Fuel per Period as the target; days since last cleaning as the input
steps.settings: Linear regression trained only on the current run since the last cleaning, inside Apples-to-Apples.
steps.output: A forecast line and the date it crosses the limit
steps.why: Lets engineers plan the next shutdown or cleaning before fouling gets too costly.

steps.inputs: Daily cost and forecast date
steps.settings: Colour thresholds for daily extra cost; Journal text with links to every step.
steps.output: A colour-coded table and a written record of the method

cases.title: Crystallization deviation investigation (pharma)
problem: Small-molecule drugs are made in batches. The last step turns the product into solid crystals, which are then filtered. During a commercial campaign, filtration took longer than the specification allows, in one batch more than twice as long. That is a deviation and a sign of a possible quality problem.

A deviation can threaten the whole batch. Batch failures cost millions, and restarting can take days or weeks while the team proves it understands what happened. Spreadsheets were too slow: trend differences are hard to see, the energy balance on the crystallization profile is hard to calculate in Excel, and every new time period meant rebuilding the calculations.
Data available: batch process data in OSIsoft PI, including jacket temperature, contents temperature and a noisy level signal.
cases.solution: Measure how much heat each batch gives off while it crystallizes. Different crystal forms (polymorphs) release different amounts of heat. Seeq finds the crystallization and filtration phases, works out the jacket-to-contents temperature difference, and adds it up (integrates it) over the crystallization phase. The slow-filtering batch had a clearly different heat integral, which showed it had formed the wrong polymorph. The process was then changed so the desired polymorph forms every time.
cases.sourceNote: The page names the key calculation (integral of the jacket-to-contents temperature difference during crystallization), the level filtering, the phase focus and the Organizer Topic. Tool settings, phase detection and the reference-profile comparison were worked out by the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base pages. Treat them as one sensible way to build it.

steps.inputs: Jacket temperature, contents temperature, level, batch phase tags
steps.settings: No special settings. Seeq lines up signals that are recorded at different intervals.

steps.settings: Low-pass or agile filter over about 10 minutes.
steps.why: The page says a filter was used on the noisy level. Noise would create false phase starts and stops.

steps.settings: Phase equals Crystallization. Maximum capsule duration about 12 hours.
steps.output: A Crystallization condition: one capsule per batch
steps.why: The page says analysis was focused on crystallization and filtration only.

steps.inputs: Batch phase tag or smoothed level
steps.settings: Phase equals Filtration (or level falling while the filter runs).
steps.why: Filtration time is the symptom that started the investigation.

steps.inputs: Filtration condition
steps.settings: Statistic: Duration, in hours. Timestamp at the end of the capsule.
steps.output: A Filtration Time signal, one point per batch
steps.why: Shows which batches broke the filtration specification.

steps.inputs: Contents temperature and jacket temperature
steps.settings: Contents minus jacket.
steps.why: While crystals form they release heat, so the contents run warmer than the cooling jacket. The bigger the gap, the more heat is being released.

steps.inputs: Delta T and the Crystallization condition
steps.settings: Integrate Delta T over each crystallization capsule.
steps.output: A Heat Integral per batch (°C·h), proportional to the heat released
steps.why: This is the page's key calculation. A different polymorph releases a different amount of heat, so the integral changes.

steps.tool: Capsule Time view and Reference Profile
steps.inputs: Delta T over the Crystallization capsules
steps.settings: Align all batches at the start of crystallization; build an average ±3 standard deviation band from good batches.
steps.output: An overlay with the deviated batch outside the normal band
steps.why: Makes the odd batch stand out at a glance, which was hard to see in spreadsheets.

steps.inputs: The trends, the heat integral and filtration time tables
steps.settings: Set to auto-update as new data arrives.
steps.output: A living report for engineering and production managers
steps.why: The page says the Topic updates itself and lets the whole team review events and suggest fixes.

Normal 1.5 h; deviated 3.8 h, which is 3.8 ÷ 1.5 = 2.5 times longer

mistakes: Integrating over the whole batch
Heating, filling and washing also create temperature differences. Integrate only inside the crystallization capsule.
Comparing batches on the calendar
Batches start at different times, so the curves never line up. Use Capsule Time to start every batch at zero.
Over-smoothing
A heavy filter can flatten the real heat peak. Smooth only the noisy level signal, and check the temperatures still show their peaks.

cases.title: Meter calibration management (gas "high-zero")
problem: A pipeline company bills customers from gas meters. In some cases the gas flow is not corrected for pressure and temperature. Then, at low flow, the billing meter can read zero even though a small amount of gas is still flowing. This is called "high-zero".

Gas that flows while the meter reads zero is never billed, so the pipeline company loses money. With a large number of meters, finding the ones with this problem is hard. Before Seeq, engineers combined the data by hand in spreadsheets and spent hours or days lining up timestamps.
Data available: process data (online meter readings) in OSIsoft PI, and calibration data in Microsoft SQL Server.
cases.solution: Put the calibration data and the live process data on the same timeline. Whenever the calibration data says the meter should read zero but the online reading is above zero, Seeq creates a capsule: a high-zero event. Maintenance can then recalibrate those meters. Because Seeq can use asset trees, the same calculation is swapped across every meter and shared in a Topic.

cases.title: Electrical submersible pump (ESP) up-time
problem: Many oil wells do not have enough reservoir pressure to push fluid to the surface, so an electrical submersible pump (ESP) down the well lifts it. These pumps do not always run well, and a sudden loss of flow can damage the pump. That means lost production and an expensive repair.

Simple trip logic can also stop pumps too early and lose production. The problem covers hundreds of pads and thousands of wells, so before Seeq, finding and analysing ESP failures was purely reactive.
Data available: wellhead temperature, motor current (amps) and tubing choke data in OSIsoft PI, with wells organised in OSIsoft Asset Framework.
cases.solution: Detect low-flow events from signals at the surface. When flow drops, the wellhead temperature drops, and motor amps and choke data help confirm it. One or two conditions alone were not accurate, so Seeq combines 15 conditions. Low-flow events during well tests or maintenance are ignored. Seeq also builds precursor capsules that warn before a low-flow event. The analytic is set up on historical events, then watches live data, and the asset model copies it to every well.

cases.title: Power loading reduction (grid operator)
problem: An independent system operator (ISO) balances power supply and demand on the grid, but does not own the power plants or wires. When the real-time power price jumps, big commercial users switch to their own generators or shut equipment down for several minutes or more, so the grid load drops sharply.

When the price falls back, that load comes back. The ISO must have enough generation ready, or there could be outages. This ISO runs the grid for 30 million people in a South-western U.S. state, with about 100 engineers and data scientists in the control room. Before Seeq, operators guessed how much load would return.
Data available: load and price signals in OSIsoft PI, with the asset hierarchy in PI AF.
cases.solution: Find every load drop caused by a price spike and measure how big it was. Seeq cleans the load signal, compares it with a delayed copy of itself to catch sudden drops (the page calls this a feed-forward), finds price spikes, and keeps only the drops that happen with a price spike. A scorecard gives the size of each drop, so operators know how much load will come back when the price returns to normal.

cases.title: Predicting product properties from reactor data (polymer viscosity)
problem: Chemical makers sort finished product into quality grades using lab tests. The best grade sells for the most, so making more of it means more revenue.

Lab tests take time and are done only every few hours or days. When a sample fails, all material made since the last good sample is downgraded, and the material still in process is likely to fail too. A large polymer producer wanted to predict product viscosity from what was happening upstream in the reactors, so it could act before off-spec product was made.
Data available: reactor sensor data in a process historian (for example OSIsoft PI, Honeywell PHD or AspenTech IP21) and lab results in a LIMS.
cases.solution: Build a soft sensor: a model that estimates viscosity all the time from reactor temperature, monomer conversion and modifier feed rate. Seeq smooths those signals, shifts them in time to allow for the delay between the reactor and the sample point, and fits a model with the Prediction tool. Spec limits are added, past excursions are found, and Seeq checks how often the model saw the excursion coming. A scorecard turns that into money.

cases.title: Field-wide analysis of Coriolis meter drive gain
problem: In an oil field, separators split oil, water and gas. When separation goes wrong, gas can escape with the liquid (gas blowby) or liquid can go out with the gas (liquid carryover). Engineers need to know quickly so they can fix it.

Coriolis flow meters are common because they cope with sand, debris and gas coming out of the liquid. Their Drive Gain (the percentage of input power the meter needs to keep its tubes vibrating) rises when there is gas in the liquid or the meter is badly calibrated. One engineer may have hundreds of meters per area to watch, so checking them by hand is not possible.
Data available: meter data, including Drive Gain, from Ignition SCADA.

The script runs every morning and makes a new set of ranked worksheets, worst meter at the top.

cases.title: Solar plant: axis tracking and soiling losses
problem: A solar plant makes less power when its panels get dirty (soiling) or when the trackers that turn the panels to follow the sun stop following their setpoint.

Plants usually use a flat, assumed loss number, based on weather and total output, to decide when cleaning panels or fixing trackers is worth it. Building a proper model of these losses was hard, or needed expensive special software that did not allow tuning or quick one-off analysis.
Data available: tracker positions and setpoints, plant output and meteorology instruments, in a Wonderware historian.
cases.solution: Find the times when the plant was at its best: panels clean and trackers following their setpoints. Use those times to train a model of how much power the plant should make from the weather readings. The gap between the model and actual output is the loss. Loss during tracker faults is tracking loss; the rest is mostly soiling. Turn the loss into dollars and compare it with the cost of cleaning or repair.

problem: Power transformers are among the most critical parts of the electrical network, and a failure can cost tens of millions of dollars. Utilities want to move from maintenance on a calendar to maintenance based on each transformer's real condition.

That needs data from many places: nameplate details, diagnostic tests (oil, dissolved gas analysis and electrical tests), maintenance and financial history, and real-time data such as cooling performance. Building health analytics from all of this, for many transformers, is hard work.
Data available: load and temperature data in PI; dissolved gas analysis (DGA) lab results in a SQL database. Oil is usually sampled and sent to a lab every 1 to 4 years.

Which gases appear tells you the type of fault (arcing, overheating, partial discharge), and how fast they grow tells you how serious it is. Seeq brings the lab gas results and the PI data together, applies standard industry methods (IEEE C57.104 Total Dissolved Combustible Gas, IEC 60599, Rogers ratio, Doernenburg, Duval triangle) in Formula, flags problems with Value Search, copies the analysis to every transformer with asset swapping, and shows the fleet in a Treemap.

cases.title: Online furnace conversion (ethane cracking)
problem: Ethylene is made by cracking ethane in furnaces. Conversion means how much of the ethane fed in is actually cracked. The control system (DCS) shows a predicted conversion, and operators set production rates from it.

If the prediction is too high, the plant makes less ethylene than it thinks and misses targets. If it is too low, the plant overproduces, overloading downstream units or filling storage. Checking the prediction meant an engineer calculating actual conversion by hand, offline, every time a weekly lab sample came in.
Data available: furnace process data in a historian (for example OSIsoft PI, AspenTech IP21 or Honeywell PHD), the asset hierarchy, and lab results in a LIMS.
cases.solution: Put the existing conversion calculation online. Seeq overlays lab and process data, keeps only the process values at the lab sample times, and uses Formula to call the plant's existing conversion script, so actual conversion is worked out for every lab sample. cases.title: Well interaction detection (oil sands)
problem: In oil sands, material can move underground from one well to a nearby well. This is called well interaction. Sometimes it is wanted: in CO2 enhanced oil recovery and in steam-assisted gravity drainage (SAGD), steam or CO2 is meant to move through the rock.

Sometimes it is not wanted: frack material, stimulants or water from a poor well can reach production wells, and steam can damage SAGD well liners. Operators need to detect it and act, on hundreds of pads and thousands of wells.
Data available: pressure, temperature, conductivity and steam injection in OSIsoft PI, with an OSIsoft Asset Framework structure that lists each well's neighbour wells.
cases.solution: Test every neighbouring well pair for a link. If steam injected into one well (the 'perpetrator') shows up later as a temperature change in a neighbour (the 'victim'), they are connected. Because material takes time to travel, the victim's temperature is shifted in time before comparing. A script (using Seeq's Matlab SDK) tries shifts from 4 hours to 4 days for hundreds of pairs, fits a straight-line (OLS) regression each time and keeps the best R². Pairs with R² of 0.2 or more at about an 8-hour shift are flagged.
cases.sourceNote: The page gives the signals, the neighbour-well AF structure, the time shifts, OLS regression, the Matlab SDK search over 4 hours to 4 days, the 8-hour average delay and the 0.2 R² rule. Tool settings and formulas were worked out by the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base pages. Treat them as one sensible way to build it.

cases.title: Emergency shutdown (ESD) water hammer characterization
problem: Oil collection networks have emergency shutdown (ESD) systems that close valves fast to protect the plant. But a fast valve closure suddenly stops the moving liquid and sends a pressure wave back and forth through the pipe. This is water hammer.

Water hammer can damage pipes and vessels and blow relief valves or rupture disks, with safety, reliability and environmental impacts. Operators wanted to find where it happens so they could redesign the ESD valves and equipment. Before Seeq the analysis was purely reactive, because there were too many wells and too much data for normal tools.
Data available: well pressure and ESD data in OSIsoft PI, with wells organised in OSIsoft Asset Framework.
cases.solution: Look for the fingerprint of water hammer right after each ESD trip: pressure peaks that repeat at a steady interval and get smaller each time. Seeq calculates the slope of the pressure, marks each local peak, checks that the time between peaks is steady (Value Search), and measures how big the swings are (Signal from Condition). The asset model copies this to every well, so the worst-hit wells can be found and fixed.

Settings and formulas were worked out by the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base pages. Treat them as one sensible way to build it.

cases.title: Clean-in-place (CIP) optimization
problem: Clean-in-place (CIP) means cleaning pipes and tanks by pumping water and cleaning chemicals through them, without taking them apart. While a line is being cleaned it cannot produce, so shorter, consistent cleaning means more production.

Analysing CIP is hard: finding from the data when cleaning is happening, measuring results and the water and chemicals used, sharing what was learned about unusual events, and noticing when cleaning stops being consistent.
Data available: process data such as conductivity, flows and valve states in OSIsoft PI, with cleaning circuits organised in PI Asset Framework.
cases.solution: Build one model of the cleaning process and apply it to every cleaning circuit, adding circuit-specific details. Seeq makes capsules for each phase (production and cleaning), calculates time and percent per phase, cleaning time and peak conductivity in each cleaning cycle, and compares cycles and circuits. cases.title: Root cause oscillation diagnosis (Causality Add-on)
problem: When a key process signal keeps oscillating, control engineers need to find where it starts. In a modern plant with hundreds of measurements, recycles and heat integration hide the path the variation takes, so looking at trends by eye can be impossible.

This example uses a published dataset from an industrial minerals concentrator. An oscillation started just upstream of the first cells in the flotation circuit, and the automatic control strategy then spread it through the whole circuit.
Data available: process historian data (for example OSIsoft PI or PHD); here, the published concentrator dataset.
cases.solution: Use the Seeq Causality Add-on to draw a causal map. It uses a statistical method that goes beyond correlation: correlation only shows that two signals move together with a time lag, while causality tries to say which one drives the other. On the map, each circle is a signal and arrows show causal flow; large blue circles are the most independent signals (likely causes) and small red circles the most dependent (effects). Trying several sensitivity settings and seeing which cause keeps coming out on top gives a consensus root cause.
cases.sourceNote: The page describes the dataset preparation, the add-on's preprocessing and downselection steps, the map colours, the sensitivity sweep and Organizer reporting. The Formula example and the worked numbers were added by the notebook. Treat them as one sensible way to use the add-on.

steps.why: Shows the direction of influence, which correlation cannot.

steps.why: The page says varying the parameters across the range finds the consensus root cause.

cases.title: Detect valve erosion and predict failure
problem: Fluids slowly wear away (erode) the inside of valves. It is hard to see this by watching single readings such as flow, valve position or pressure, because the control loop keeps adjusting and hides the change.
So valves fail without warning. Failures risk workers' health, plant safety and the environment (loss of containment), and quickly add costs from unplanned maintenance and lost production.
Data available: process data (flow, valve position, pressures) in OSIsoft PI and maintenance records in SAP.
cases.solution: Use first-principles valve physics. The flow coefficient (Cv) says how much flow a valve passes for a given pressure drop. Seeq calculates the valve's actual (operating) Cv from flow and pressure drop, and compares it with the Cv it should have at that position (theoretical Cv). As the valve erodes, it passes more flow than it should, so operating Cv drifts above theoretical. Seeq flags gaps over ±10 %, and a Prediction model trained on past failures projects the gap forward to estimate the failure date and the best maintenance date, so bad actors are fixed first.
cases.sourceNote: The page lists the Agile Filter, downtime removal, the operating versus theoretical Cv and Delta Cv in Formula, the ±10 % Boundaries and Value Search, the Prediction model trained on past failures, and the Organizer tables. The Cv equation, the theoretical curve and the numbers were added by the notebook. Treat them as one sensible way to build it.
