cases.title: Steel coil processing: scheduling and performance
problem: A large flat-rolled steel company processes steel coils through steps such as loading and threading. Management wanted better daily production goals, more accurate scheduling and faster troubleshooting of delays.

The insights are hard to get because the processing data has to be combined with relational data such as each coil's product properties, then cleansed, totalled and grouped in different ways. Typical analysis tools do not combine time-series and relational data like this.
Data available: processing data in a historian (for example OSIsoft PI, AspenTech IP21 or Honeywell PHD) and product properties in a SQL database.
cases.solution: Turn each processing step for each coil into a capsule, attach the coil's product properties to it, and split the results by operator shift. Then compare step times by operator and by product, and set daily goals from real processing times instead of one flat number.
cases.sourceNote: The page names the step capsules, product properties as condition properties, condition filtering by operator shift, and regular dashboard reviews. The signals, limits and formulas below were worked out by the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base pages. Treat them as one sensible way to build it.

steps.inputs: Line speed, motor current and other line signals; coil records with grade, gauge and width
steps.settings: Bring coil records in as a condition (one capsule per coil) carrying the properties.
steps.output: Line signals and a Coils condition with properties
steps.why: The page's key challenge is combining process data with relational product data.

steps.inputs: Line speed (and uncoiler signals)
steps.settings: Line stopped while the uncoiler is being loaded; ignore very short gaps; maximum duration 2 hours.
steps.why: Each step needs its own capsules to be timed.

steps.inputs: Line speed
steps.settings: Slow speed band used while threading (for example between 1 and 15 m/min) for at least a few seconds.
steps.why: Threading is a common source of delay.

steps.n: Attach product properties to each step
steps.inputs: Loading and Threading conditions; the Coils condition
steps.settings: Copy grade, gauge and width from the coil capsule onto each step capsule.
steps.output: Step capsules that know which product they were
steps.why: The page says product properties were integrated as condition properties, so delays can be split by product.

steps.inputs: Shift schedule and the step capsules
steps.settings: 8-hour shifts at the plant's shift times in its time zone; give each step capsule its shift or operator.
steps.why: The page used condition filtering to separate performance by operator (shift).

steps.inputs: Loading and Threading conditions
steps.settings: Statistic: duration in minutes, one value per coil.
steps.output: Loading Time and Threading Time per coil
steps.why: Turns steps into numbers that can be averaged and compared.

steps.inputs: Step capsules with operator and grade
steps.settings: Average duration grouped by operator, then by grade.
steps.output: Bar charts of step time by operator and grade
steps.why: Shows whether delays come from the operator or from hard-to-process products, so gaps drive training and staffing.

steps.inputs: Step times and coil counts per shift
steps.settings: Colour thresholds; goals set per grade from actual times; reviewed regularly.
steps.why: The page says dashboard reports were regularly reviewed and goals became realistic.

example.caption: Six coils in one 8-hour shift (made-up numbers, minutes: load, thread, run)
rows: A: load 7.3, thread 6.7. B: load 13.7, thread 14.0. B is slower, but B also had more grade Y, so compare within a grade
All grade X: 480 ÷ 65 = about 7 coils. All grade Y: 480 ÷ 94 = about 5 coils
example.note: All numbers are made up for teaching. The page gives no times or goals.

mistakes: One goal for every product
Hard grades take longer. Set goals from actual times per grade.
Blaming operators for product effects
If one shift gets harder grades, its times look worse. Compare operators within the same grade.
Counting stoppages as threading
Crane waits or breakdowns inflate step times. Remove downtime first.
cases.reported: With the dashboards reviewed regularly: scheduling became more accurate, with daily production goals set more consistently and realistically from actual data and differentiated by several variables; significant processing delays linked to operators and product properties were addressed more quickly; gaps in operator performance became visible, driving training, sharing of best practices and staffing changes. As these items are addressed, the analytics can be used for deeper opportunities in processing steps and sequencing of customer orders. The page gives no figures.
cases.assumptions: The page does not say which signals define each step, the shift pattern or any times. All numbers are placeholders.

cases.title: Operators find production settings for grade changes
problem: When a plant changes from one product grade to another, operators must choose the production settings. They usually look them up in a written logbook from the last time that grade was made.

The logbook may record quality or other KPIs, but not the full story of the last run: they are numbers on paper, not trends showing how settings and KPIs moved together. Operators often just copy the settings from the end of the last run, which leads to a lot of off-spec product after the grade change.
Data available: grade, process settings and quality or rate signals in the plant historian. The page does not name the historian.
cases.solution: Give operators the whole previous campaign, not one number. Seeq makes a condition for the production runs of each grade (with Value Search), so operators can jump to past runs of the grade they are about to make, see the trends of settings against quality and production rate, and choose startup settings that worked well across the whole run.
cases.sourceNote: The page is short: it names Value Search for production runs, navigating to past runs, and viewing settings against KPIs. The in-spec search, Capsule Time overlay and scorecard were added by the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base pages. Treat them as one sensible way to build it.

steps.n: Mark each run of a grade
steps.inputs: Product grade signal
steps.settings: Grade equals the one you are about to make (for example Grade B); ignore very short flickers during changeovers.
steps.why: The page defines production runs with Value Search. Each past campaign becomes a capsule you can jump to.

steps.inputs: Quality signal (online analyser or lab result)
steps.settings: Between the lower and upper spec limits (for example 12 and 15).
steps.why: Separates good product from off-spec product inside each run.

steps.inputs: Grade B Runs and In Spec
steps.settings: Intersection (A and B).
steps.why: Shows only the settings that actually made good product.

steps.inputs: Settings, quality and rate over the Grade B Runs
steps.settings: Align runs at their start; colour each run differently.
steps.output: Past runs side by side from startup
steps.why: The page wants operators to see the relationship between settings and quality or rate across the whole run.

steps.inputs: Grade B Runs and In Spec
steps.settings: Time from run start to the first in-spec capsule, per run.
steps.output: A Time to Spec value for each past run
steps.why: Points to the runs whose startup settings worked best.

steps.inputs: Key settings during in-spec periods and Time to Spec
steps.settings: One row per past run: setting values at startup and average while in spec, and time to spec.
steps.output: A table operators check before a grade change
steps.why: Replaces searching the paper logbook.

example.caption: Last run of grade B, spec 12 to 15 (made-up numbers)
rows: Reactor 185 °C, feed pressure 20 bar, quality 8.0: off spec
175 °C, 22 bar, quality 13.5: in spec, near the middle
168 °C, 25 bar, quality 12.1: in spec but near the low limit, after late-run drift such as fouling
Start near the middle-of-run settings (175 °C, 22 bar), not the end-of-run values written in the logbook
example.note: All numbers are made up for teaching. The page gives no settings or quality values.

mistakes: Copying end-of-run settings
Late in a run the plant has drifted (for example fouling). Those settings rarely suit a fresh start.
Scrolling raw trends
Finding old runs by hand takes too long. Let Value Search make the run capsules.
No minimum duration
Brief grade-tag flickers during changeovers create false runs. Ignore short capsules.
cases.reported: With access to these analytics, operators can reduce off-spec production when changing grades, choose better startup settings by considering the whole previous campaign instead of just the last value, and spend less time writing settings in logbooks and searching through them. The page gives no figures.
cases.assumptions: The page does not name the signals, the spec limits or the plant. It assumes the product grade is recorded as a signal. All numbers are placeholders.

cases.title: Truck fleet monitoring (mining haul trucks)
problem: Big haul trucks carry material from the bottom of a mine to the surface. Each one is worth more than $3 million, they work in extreme conditions, and engine trouble is common. Unplanned truck downtime is expensive.

Mines usually service trucks on a calendar, which still lets some trucks break down and wastes time and money on trucks that are fine. Telemetry can show engine problems for one truck, but signal availability, sample rate and size vary from truck to truck, so scaling to the whole fleet is hard.
Data available: truck telemetry in OSIsoft PI, organised in OSIsoft Asset Framework.
cases.solution: A truck with a weak engine climbs out of the mine slowly. Seeq measures each truck's travel time from the bottom to the top, flags trips that take too long (ignoring delays such as mandatory operator breaks), and checks whether gear, engine load, payload, throttle and ground speed also deviate from their normal (reference) profiles. Trucks with both a long climb and deviations are flagged, and a Treemap shows the whole fleet so maintenance can focus on trucks that really need it.
cases.sourceNote: The page lists the cleansing, the travel-time calculation, the excessive-travel condition, reference profiles for five signals, the composite condition, the Treemap and the live Organizer document. Signals used to detect trips and breaks, limits and formulas were worked out by the notebook. Treat them as one sensible way to build it.

steps.inputs: Truck telemetry signals
steps.settings: Remove invalid points from communication dropouts or sensor calibration.
steps.why: The page says invalid data is removed; dropouts would make fake slow trips.

steps.inputs: Location or elevation, and ground speed
steps.settings: From leaving the bottom of the pit to arriving at the top while loaded.
steps.output: A Climb condition: one capsule per trip up
steps.why: Travel time can only be measured once each trip is marked.

steps.inputs: Climb condition
steps.settings: Statistic: duration, in minutes.
steps.why: The page calculates travel time from the base to the top of the mine.

steps.inputs: Speed and parking brake (or break schedule)
steps.settings: Mark stops such as mandatory operator breaks; subtract their time from the climb.
steps.why: The page says excessive times caused by non-engine issues such as operator breaks are excluded.

steps.inputs: Net Climb Time
steps.settings: Greater than a limit, for example 40 minutes.
steps.why: The page creates a condition for excessive travel times.

steps.inputs: Gear, engine load, payload, throttle and ground speed over climbs from healthy periods
steps.settings: Average with upper and lower limits (for example ±2 standard deviations).
steps.output: Reference profiles and limits for the five signals
steps.why: The page builds reference profiles for these five signals to judge truck health.

steps.inputs: Long Travel and profile deviations
steps.settings: Long Travel AND (engine load above limit OR speed below limit, and so on).
steps.why: The page combines deviations with long travel times so slow trips caused by traffic are not blamed on the engine.

steps.inputs: Maintenance Flag for every truck in the asset tree
steps.settings: Treemap coloured red for flagged trucks; Organizer set as a live document.
steps.output: A fleet health map and a live report
steps.why: The page scales across hundreds of trucks with a Treemap and uses a live Organizer document to notify the Operations Center in near real time.

example.caption: Three trucks (made-up numbers; normal climb 30 min, limit 40 min; normal engine load 80–90 %, speed 15–20 mph)
rows: Climb 28 min; load 84 %; speed 18 mph: healthy
Climb 52 min, but 20 min was an operator break: net 52 − 20 = 32 min; load and speed normal: not flagged
Climb 48 min, no breaks; load 96 % (above 90) and speed 10 mph (below 15): flagged for maintenance
example.note: All numbers and limits are made up for teaching. The page gives no times or limits.

mistakes: Not removing breaks and queues
Waiting time looks like a weak engine. Subtract non-engine delays first.
Using travel time alone
Traffic or road conditions also slow trucks. Confirm with engine load, throttle, gear and speed profiles.
One limit for every truck
Telemetry differs between trucks. Build profiles per truck or truck model.
cases.reported: The Seeq visualisation shows all trucks in the fleet that have a maintenance condition before a failure happens. Preventing a single truck failure saves about $100,000 in parts, labour and lost opportunity, with significant fleet-wide savings. With the analysis and Treemap, the mine greatly reduced the time needed to analyse trucks for preventive maintenance, eliminated periodically scheduled truck maintenance, and now focuses on the vehicles that truly need service, a major saving of engineer and mechanic time and effort.
cases.assumptions: The page does not give the trip detection method, the travel time limit, profile limits or how breaks are recognised. All numbers are placeholders.

cases.title: Calculating KPIs during heats (steel arc furnace)
problem: In an electric arc furnace, each batch of steel is called a heat. A steel company wanted KPIs and quality indicators for every heat.
There are so many heats that calculating the KPIs by hand took a lot of work in Excel, leaving the engineers little or no time to analyse the data and make better production decisions.
Data available: furnace data in an Ignition historian (including a heat number signal) and lab (LIMS) data in SQL.
cases.solution: Let Seeq find every heat from the heat number signal and calculate the KPIs automatically. For each heat Seeq measures metrics such as power-on time (how long the furnace is melting), adds lab results, and rolls the KPIs up per shift. Ideal heats form a reference profile, and a deviation search flags heats where power-on time is above the recommended limit, so engineers can tell long-term drift from one-off problems. An Organizer Topic is updated every morning.
cases.sourceNote: The page names To Condition for heats, Value Search for power on, Signal from Condition for power-on time, Deviation Search against the limit, reference profiles from ideal heats, shift metrics and a daily Organizer Topic. Settings, limits and formulas were worked out by the notebook from the Seeq Knowledge Base pages. Treat them as one sensible way to build it.

steps.inputs: Heat number signal
steps.settings: A new capsule each time the heat number changes, with the heat number kept as a property.
steps.why: The page identifies each heat from the heat number signal; every KPI is then calculated per heat.

steps.inputs: LIMS results from SQL, bounded by Heats
steps.settings: Take the lab value(s) inside each heat.
steps.why: The page combines historian signals and lab data in the heat metrics.

steps.inputs: Furnace power
steps.settings: Power above a small threshold; ignore short dips; maximum duration 2 hours.
steps.why: The page uses Value Search to identify the power-on condition.

steps.inputs: Power On, bounded by Heats
steps.settings: Statistic: total duration in minutes. Timestamp at the start of the heat.
steps.output: A Power-On Time signal, one value per heat
steps.why: The page uses Signal from Condition for power-on time per heat.

steps.inputs: Power-On Time and the recommended limit
steps.settings: Above the recommended limit (for example 40 minutes).
steps.why: The page uses deviation search to find when power-on time is above the recommended limit.

steps.inputs: A key signal (such as power) over heats chosen as ideal
steps.settings: Average with upper and lower boundaries.
steps.output: Normal operating boundaries through a heat
steps.why: The page uses ideal heats and the reference profile tool to see when operation goes outside boundaries.

steps.inputs: Boundary exceedances and Over Limit heats over weeks
steps.settings: Count exceedances over time; overlay heats from their start.
steps.output: A view of whether exceedances are growing or isolated
steps.why: The page tracks exceedances to see long-term drift versus one-off deviations.

steps.tool: Periodic Condition, Scorecard Metric and Organizer Topic
steps.inputs: Per-heat KPIs
steps.settings: Shifts as capsules; averages and counts per shift; Topic updated each morning.
steps.output: A daily report for the team
steps.why: The page rolls KPIs up per shift and sends an Organizer Topic every morning.

example.caption: Four heats in one shift, recommended limit 40 minutes (made-up numbers)
rows: Check heat 103 first; if over-limit heats keep rising week by week, it is drift, not a one-off
example.note: All numbers and the limit are made up for teaching. The page gives no times or limits.

mistakes: Short power dips splitting capsules
Brief dips during tapping or charging break power-on into pieces. Ignore short gaps in Value Search.
Comparing heats on the calendar
Heats start at different times. Use Capsule Time so each starts at zero.
Reference profile from noisy raw data
Noise makes the boundaries wide or jumpy. Use clean data and only truly ideal heats.
cases.reported: The company built an Organizer Topic that is updated each morning, so the team can see daily performance and make per-shift corrections to optimise the time spent in each stage of operation. Work that took hours in Excel spreadsheets is now updated and sent to the team automatically. Plant leadership can quickly see the last day's performance and focus on boundary excursions to troubleshoot over the next shift. The page gives no figures.
cases.assumptions: The page does not give the power threshold, the recommended limit, the KPIs beyond power-on time or the shift pattern. All numbers are placeholders.
